title: Northmere Food Safety Code overview
note: The Northmere Food Safety Code is the regulatory regime that governs how Brackenridge Provisions makes and ships chilled ready meals and soups. It sets out duties for hazard analysis, hygiene, allergen handling, record keeping and reporting. The code is enforced by the Northmere Food Standards Office, which can inspect without notice, request records and suspend a plant licence when serious failures are found.

title: Relationship with the Northmere Food Standards Office
note: The Northmere Food Standards Office, usually shortened to NFSO, is the regulator that licenses both Brackenridge plants. Our named liaison officer changes every few years. All formal correspondence goes through the compliance mailbox so that there is a single trail of what was sent, when, and by whom. Informal phone calls are summarised in writing the same day.

title: Brackenridge Provisions compliance programme
note: Brackenridge Provisions runs a compliance programme that covers two production sites, Ellery Road and Pennick Moor. The programme brings together hazard analysis, internal audits, supplier approval, training, traceability and regulatory filings. A quarterly compliance committee chaired by the operations director reviews open findings, overdue actions and any upcoming changes to the code.

title: Annual hygiene return filing deadline
note: Each plant must submit its annual hygiene return to the regulator by 31 March. The return summarises cleaning verification results, pest activity, staff training completion and any incidents from the previous calendar year. Late filing triggers an automatic warning letter, and a second late filing in three years can lead to an unannounced inspection. The compliance lead drafts the return in February so the plant managers have time to check figures.

title: Hazard analysis plan for chilled soups
note:
The hazard analysis plan for chilled soups is the core document that explains how Brackenridge identifies and controls food safety hazards across the soup lines at Pennick Moor. It was first written when the soup range launched and has been revised every time a recipe family, piece of equipment or packaging format changed. The plan follows the classic structure of describing the product, mapping the process, listing hazards at each step, deciding which steps are critical, and setting limits, monitoring, corrective actions and verification for each of them.

The product description covers more than forty recipes grouped into three families: clear broths, blended vegetable soups and soups containing meat or dairy. Each family has a slightly different risk profile. Blended vegetable soups carry a higher risk from soil-borne spores because root vegetables arrive with more dirt, while the dairy family carries a higher risk from heat-resistant bacteria and from allergen cross-contact. The intended use is that consumers reheat the soup, but the plan assumes some people will eat it cold or only warm it slightly, so safety cannot depend on the reheating step.

The process map starts at goods in, where vegetables, stocks, cream and spices are received and checked. It continues through washing, peeling, chopping, kettle cooking, blending, hot filling into pots, sealing, chilling, labelling, case packing and cold storage. Every step on the map was walked by the hazard analysis team with the line supervisor present, because the drawings in the engineering office had drifted from what actually happens on the floor. Two undocumented hoses and a manual top-up step for seasoning were found during the last walk and added to the map.

Hazards are listed in three groups. Biological hazards include pathogens that survive cooking, spores that germinate if cooling is slow, and contamination introduced after cooking from surfaces or people. Chemical hazards include cleaning residues, allergen cross-contact and lubricant from the blender gearbox. Physical hazards include metal from worn blades, plastic from broken scoops and glass from the inspection lamps above the filler. For each hazard the team records likelihood and severity and explains the reasoning in plain language so a new reader can follow it.

The critical control points for soups are kettle cooking, chilling and metal detection. Kettle cooking must reach the core temperature set out in the cooking requirement and is monitored with calibrated probes logged every batch. Metal detection runs on every pot and is challenged with test pieces at the start of each shift. Chilling is the step that has caused the most discussion over the years, because slow cooling allows spores to germinate and multiply, and soups are dense liquids that hold heat for a long time inside large pots.

The general chilling limit in the plan is that soup must fall from 63 degrees to 8 degrees within 90 minutes of filling. Line 3 at Pennick Moor, which fills the one litre family pots, holds a written derogation that allows 105 minutes instead, granted after a validation study showed that the larger pot geometry could not meet 90 minutes without freezing the outer layer. The derogation is conditional on a reduced shelf life for those pots and on the blast chiller door staying shut for the whole cycle.

Verification of the plan happens in several ways. Monitoring records are reviewed daily by the shift quality technician, weekly by the quality manager, and sampled during internal audits. The full plan is formally reviewed once a year and whenever a significant change is proposed. Any deviation from a critical limit is treated as a nonconformance, the affected product is held, and the release decision is taken by the quality manager rather than by production.

title: Critical control point monitoring
note: Critical control point monitoring is the routine checking of the few process steps where a failure would make food unsafe. At Brackenridge these are cooking, chilling and metal detection. Operators record readings on the line terminal, and any reading outside its limit locks the batch until a quality technician reviews it. Monitoring frequency is set in the hazard analysis plan and cannot be reduced without committee approval.

title: Cooking core temperature of 75 degrees for 30 seconds
note: Every cooked batch must reach a core temperature of at least 75 degrees and hold it for 30 seconds. The reading is taken with a calibrated probe at the slowest heating point of the kettle or oven, which was identified during heat mapping. If the target is missed the batch is cooked again or discarded, and the event is logged as a deviation.

title: Metal fragments from worn mixer blades
note: The large mixers at Ellery Road use stainless blades that wear over time. A chipped blade could shed small metal fragments into product. The metal detectors should catch most of these, but very thin slivers may pass. Engineering inspects blades weekly and replaces them on a fixed schedule rather than waiting for visible damage.

title: Metal detectors on packing lines
note: Each packing line has an inline metal detector placed after sealing. The detectors are tuned for ferrous, non-ferrous and stainless test pieces of set sizes. At the start of every shift and after any line stoppage, an operator passes the test pieces through to prove the reject mechanism works. Failed checks mean all product since the last good check is held.

title: Reject-to-locked-bin on metal detector trips
note: We decided that every metal detector must reject packs into a locked bin that only quality staff can open. Previously rejects dropped into an open tray and were occasionally put back on the line by mistake. The locked bin removes that temptation and gives a clean count of rejects for trend analysis.

title: Internal audit programme
note: The internal audit programme checks that each plant follows its own food safety procedures between external inspections. Audits are scheduled across the year so every area is covered at least annually, with high-risk areas such as high-care production and allergen handling visited more often. Findings are graded as minor, major or critical and tracked to closure in the corrective action tracker.

title: Internal audit methodology
note:
This note describes how Brackenridge plans, carries out and reports internal food safety audits. The aim of the methodology is consistency: two different auditors looking at the same area on the same day should reach broadly the same conclusions and grade findings in the same way. It also aims to make audits useful for the people being audited rather than a box-ticking exercise they dread.

Planning starts with the annual audit calendar, built each December by the compliance lead. The calendar lists every process area and every procedure in the food safety manual and assigns each one a risk rating. High-risk areas such as high-care production, allergen changeover and goods-in temperature checks are audited at least three times a year. Medium-risk areas are audited twice a year and low-risk areas such as office document control once a year. The calendar is shared with plant managers so they can flag clashes with major production runs, but the dates are not negotiable once confirmed.

Before an audit, the lead auditor reads the relevant procedures, previous findings for that area, recent deviations and any customer complaints linked to it. They prepare a short checklist, but the checklist is a prompt rather than a script. Auditors are encouraged to follow trails: if a cleaning record looks odd, they trace it back to the chemical stores log, the training record of the person who signed it, and the verification swab result. Many of the most valuable findings in past years came from following a trail rather than from the checklist itself.

During the audit the auditor spends most of the time on the floor, observing work, asking operators to explain what they are doing and why, and comparing what they see with what the procedure says. Interviews are kept short and friendly. Auditors avoid asking leading questions and do not tell operators the right answer during the interview. Evidence is recorded as it is found, with photographs where useful, and every potential finding is discussed with the area supervisor before the auditor leaves so there are no surprises in the report.

Grading follows a simple rule set. A critical finding is one where unsafe food has been produced or is likely to be produced. A major finding is a breakdown of a control that has not yet resulted in unsafe food. A minor finding is an isolated lapse or a documentation gap. Auditors must write each finding as a clear statement of what was expected, what was found and why it matters. Vague findings such as poor housekeeping are sent back for rewriting before the report is issued.

Auditor independence is protected by a specific rule. Nobody may audit a department in which they have worked at any time during the previous 18 months, and this includes temporary cover and secondments, not only permanent roles. The compliance lead checks the rule when assigning auditors each quarter, and any exception has to be approved in writing by the operations director with the reason recorded on the audit file.

Reports are issued within five working days of the audit. The report goes to the area manager, the plant manager and the compliance lead. Area managers must propose corrective actions with owners and dates within ten working days, and the findings then follow the normal closure timelines. Trends across audits are reviewed at the quarterly compliance committee so that recurring weaknesses lead to wider changes rather than repeated local fixes.

title: Rotate internal auditors between plants
note: Auditors from Ellery Road audit Pennick Moor and the other way round. We chose this so that people see the other site with fresh eyes and so that familiarity does not soften findings. Travel adds cost, so each auditor covers a full day of areas per visit.

title: Audit findings closed within 60 days
note: Minor and major internal audit findings must be closed within 60 days of the report. Critical findings must have an immediate containment action on the day and a full fix within 14 days. Closure needs evidence such as a photograph, a revised record or a retraining sign-off, not just a statement that the work is done.

title: Repeat findings on allergen cleaning
note: Allergen cleaning at Ellery Road has produced similar findings in three consecutive audits, usually around incomplete swab records after changeovers. Repeat findings suggest the fix has not addressed the root cause. If the regulator sees the same pattern it could escalate to formal enforcement.

title: Allergen management across both plants
note: Allergen management covers how Brackenridge stops the fourteen regulated allergens from ending up in products that do not declare them. It includes segregated storage, colour-coded utensils, production scheduling that runs allergen-free recipes first, validated cleaning between products and label checks at packing.

title: Allergen changeover validated with swab tests
note: After a changeover from an allergen-containing product, the line must be cleaned to the written method and then tested with rapid protein swabs at defined points. Production of the next product cannot start until the swabs pass. The swab locations were chosen from a study of where residues collect, such as filler nozzles and conveyor joints.

title: Dedicated line for sesame products
note: We decided to move all sesame-containing products onto a single dedicated line at Pennick Moor. Sesame paste proved very hard to clean from the shared fillers, and swab failures were common. A dedicated line costs some flexibility but removes the most persistent cross-contact problem.

title: Should mustard be handled on shared lines?
note: Mustard currently appears in four recipes produced on shared lines. Cleaning has worked so far, but a customer has asked whether we can guarantee mustard-free status for their own range. Do we keep sharing, schedule mustard runs at the end of the week, or invest in another dedicated line?

title: Allergen label review procedure
note:
The allergen label review procedure exists because the most common cause of food recalls across the industry is not contamination but incorrect labelling. A product can be made perfectly and still be dangerous if the pack says it contains no milk when it does. At Brackenridge this procedure governs how labels are designed, approved, printed, loaded onto lines and checked during packing.

Label design starts from the approved recipe specification, which lists every ingredient and sub-ingredient along with its allergen content. The technical team builds the ingredient declaration directly from the specification rather than typing it by hand, so that a recipe change cannot be missed. Allergens are emphasised in bold in the declaration, and a separate may contain statement is only added when a documented risk assessment shows that cross-contact cannot be controlled. We do not use precautionary statements as a general safety blanket because they make labels less useful for people with allergies.

Approval of a new or changed label needs three signatures: the technical manager who checked the declaration against the specification, the marketing owner who checked the brand content, and a quality technician who compared the final print proof against the approved artwork. Any change to a proof after approval, even a change of font size, restarts the approval. Approved artwork is stored in the document vault with a version number that is printed in small type on the label itself, so the version can be checked on the line.

Printing is done on site using thermal printers for date codes and pre-printed label rolls for the main artwork. Rolls arrive from the label supplier with a reel certificate showing the artwork version, and goods-in staff check the version against the approved list before the rolls go into stock. Obsolete rolls are destroyed rather than kept as spares, because old rolls in a cupboard were the cause of a near miss two years ago when a superseded label without a new allergen was loaded during a busy night.

On the line, the operator loading a label roll scans the barcode on the reel and the line terminal checks it against the product scheduled for that run. A mismatch stops the line. At start-up and every hour, a packing operator takes a finished pack and compares the label against the product being made, including the allergen declaration, and records the check. When a run changes product, the old rolls are removed from the line area completely before the new rolls are brought in, so that only one label type is ever present at a station.

Two-person checks are used at the highest-risk moments: the first pack of every run and the first pack after any roll change. One person reads the label aloud while the other compares it against the schedule. This is slow but has caught errors that a single person missed. Labels printed during the night shift need the morning quality lead's signature before dispatch. As an extra safeguard, the Ellery Road date-code printer locks itself after 40 unreconciled labels, meaning that if forty printed labels cannot be matched to packs on the line count, printing stops until a supervisor investigates where they went.

The procedure is audited three times a year and is part of every external inspection. Any labelling error that reaches a customer, even without an allergen, is treated as a major incident and investigated by the technical manager.

title: Record retention rules
note: Record retention rules set how long each kind of food safety record must be kept and in what form. The code sets minimum periods, and Brackenridge sometimes keeps records longer for customer contracts or legal reasons. The retention schedule lists every record type, its owner, its storage location and its destruction date.

title: Temperature logs retained for three years
note: All cooking, chilling and cold storage temperature logs must be kept for three years from the date of production. This covers the full shelf life of every product plus the period in which the regulator might reasonably investigate a complaint. Logs older than three years are securely destroyed in January each year after the compliance lead signs off the destruction list.

title: Supplier certificates retained for five years
note: Certificates of analysis and supplier approval documents are kept for five years after the supplier relationship ends. This longer period reflects customer contract terms and the fact that supplier issues can surface long after the ingredients were used.

title: Move paper records to the document vault
note: We decided to scan paper production records into the electronic document vault at the end of each week and to stop keeping paper archives on site. The vault is searchable, backed up offsite and access controlled. Paper originals are kept for ninety days after scanning in case a scan is poor.

title: Scanned records not legible enough for inspectors
note: Some handwritten records scan poorly, especially pencil entries and forms that got wet on the line. If an inspector cannot read a scanned record, it may be treated as missing. The ninety day paper overlap only helps if someone checks scan quality before the originals are destroyed.

title: Release of retained records to the regulator
note: When the regulator formally requests documents, Brackenridge must hand over the relevant retained records in a usable form. This release of records is a legal obligation rather than a courtesy. Requests are logged, the compliance lead decides what falls within scope, and copies are sent through the secure transfer service with a cover index of every file provided.

title: Records released to the regulator within five working days
note: Records requested by the Northmere Food Standards Office must be supplied within five working days unless the officer agrees a longer period in writing. Urgent requests linked to a suspected outbreak must be answered the same day, even if only partly, with the rest following as soon as possible.

title: Records request handling procedure
note:
This procedure explains how Brackenridge responds when the Northmere Food Standards Office, a retail customer, or a court asks for food safety records. It applies to paper and electronic records, emails and photographs, and to records held by contractors on our behalf such as the pest control company and the external laboratory. The goal is to respond quickly and completely while protecting information that we are entitled to keep private.

Every request is logged the moment it arrives, regardless of how it arrives. Some requests come by formal letter, some by email to the compliance mailbox and some verbally during an inspection. Verbal requests are written down, read back to the officer and confirmed by email within the hour so that both sides agree what was asked. The log records the requester, the date, the deadline, the scope and the person responsible for the response.

Scoping is the most important step. The compliance lead reads the request carefully and decides which record types, dates, products and sites are covered. When the request is ambiguous, we ask for clarification in writing rather than guessing, because answering a narrower question than the one asked can look like concealment, while answering a much broader one can expose unrelated material and waste days of effort. The scope decision is recorded in the log with a short explanation.

Collection is done by the record owners listed in the retention schedule. Each owner searches their systems and returns copies with a short note confirming what they searched and how. For electronic systems, exports are taken in their native format where possible, with a readable copy alongside. For paper records still within the ninety day overlap, both the scan and the original are checked. Contractors are asked to supply their records directly to the compliance lead rather than through the plant, so that the chain is clear.

Before anything leaves the building, a second person reviews the bundle against the scope. They check that every requested item is either included or explained, that nothing outside scope has slipped in, and that personal data of staff who are not relevant is redacted. A cover index lists every file with a reference number, and the same reference is stamped on each page. A copy of the full bundle exactly as sent is kept in a locked folder in the document vault.

Some material is legitimately withheld. The most common example is legal advice from our solicitors about a dispute or investigation, which is protected by privilege. Withheld items are never simply left out. They are listed on a separate withholding schedule that describes each item in general terms and gives the reason for withholding it, and that schedule must be signed by the general counsel, currently Ottilie Varga, before the bundle is released. If she is unavailable, the bundle waits, because only the general counsel can make a privilege call on behalf of the company.

Timing is tracked against the deadline from the first day. If collection is running late, the compliance lead contacts the requester before the deadline passes, explains what is delayed and offers a partial response, rather than letting the date slip quietly.

After the response is sent, the log is updated with the date, method and reference, and any follow-up questions from the requester are handled as part of the same entry. The compliance committee reviews all requests each quarter to look for patterns, such as the same record type being hard to find, which then feeds into improvements to the retention schedule.

title: Small producer exemptions
note: The code grants certain exemptions to producers or product lines below set volume thresholds. An exempt line may follow simplified hazard analysis and filing rules. Brackenridge as a whole is too large to be exempt, but some seasonal or low-volume lines can qualify individually if they meet the conditions and are formally registered with the regulator.

title: Claim the seasonal product exemption for the winter pie range
note: We decided to register the winter pie range under the seasonal product exemption because it runs for only ten weeks a year on a separate small line. The exemption reduces the filing burden but does not change hygiene standards. The registration must be renewed every autumn before production starts.

title: Does the chutney line qualify for the low-risk exemption?
note: The chutney line makes high-acid, high-sugar products with a long ambient shelf life. These look like they meet the low-risk exemption conditions, but one recipe uses fresh garlic in oil, which may push it outside the definition. We need a ruling before claiming the exemption.

title: Exemption lapses when volume threshold is crossed
note: If an exempt line grows past the volume threshold mid-year, the exemption lapses from that point and full obligations apply immediately. Sales growth on the winter pie range could trigger this without anyone in compliance noticing, leaving us filing on the wrong basis.

title: Supplier approval process overview
note: Supplier approval is the process for deciding which ingredient and packaging suppliers Brackenridge will buy from. Suppliers are risk rated by material type and history. Approval needs a completed questionnaire, relevant certificates and, for higher-risk materials, an onsite visit. Approved suppliers are reviewed annually.

title: Supplier red flag checklist
note: The supplier red flag checklist lists warning signs that a supplier may be unreliable or dishonest. Examples include prices well below the market, reluctance to share the country of origin, certificates with mismatched dates, frequent changes of trading name and refusals to allow visits. Any single red flag triggers a review by the technical manager before the next order.

title: Annual onsite visit for high-risk suppliers
note: Suppliers of high-risk materials, such as cooked meats, dairy and spices prone to adulteration, receive an onsite visit from our technical team every year. Paper approval alone missed problems in the past. Visits are announced, but the visiting team may walk any area of the site.

title: Supplier changes ingredient source without notice
note: A supplier might switch the farm, mill or country behind an ingredient without telling us, which could introduce new allergens or contamination risks. Contracts require notice of changes, but enforcement depends on spotting differences in certificates or product behaviour.

title: Supplier approval workflow
note:
The supplier approval workflow describes, step by step, how a new supplier moves from first contact to approved status at Brackenridge, and how existing suppliers are kept under review. It was rewritten after a spice adulteration scare showed that our old process relied too heavily on paperwork supplied by the supplier and too little on our own checks.

The workflow starts when a buyer wants to source a new material or a new supplier for an existing material. The buyer raises a request in the supplier system describing the material, the expected volume, the reason for the change and any known history of the supplier. The technical team then assigns a risk rating based on the material type. Ready-to-eat ingredients, dairy, meat, spices and anything used after the cooking step are high risk. Raw vegetables and dry goods that are cooked later are medium risk. Packaging that does not touch food is low risk.

The supplier then completes our questionnaire. It covers the legal identity of the business, certifications held, hazard analysis, allergen controls, traceability, pest control, recall arrangements and the origin of raw materials. The questionnaire must be signed by a named person at the supplier who has authority to commit the business. Answers are not taken at face value. The technical team checks certifications directly with the issuing body, looks up the trading history of the company and compares the answers with the red flag checklist.

The questionnaire produces a score out of one hundred, weighted so that answers about traceability, allergen control and origin of raw materials count for more than answers about general administration. The score is used together with the risk rating to decide what happens next. Low-risk materials with a good score can be approved on paper. Medium-risk materials need a sample to be tested in our own laboratory. High-risk materials always need an onsite visit by our technical team before approval.

The onsite visit follows a standard template but leaves room for judgement. Visitors walk the full process, check a sample of traceability records by picking a finished batch and following it back to its raw materials, look at cleaning and pest control, and talk to operators. A visit report is written within a week and lists any conditions that must be met before or after approval.

Commercial teams sometimes push for faster approval, especially when a current supplier has failed and the line is short of a material. The workflow allows a temporary emergency approval for up to thirty days, but only for medium-risk materials, only with a laboratory test of the first delivery, and only with written sign-off from the technical manager.

There is one firm limit in the workflow that cannot be overridden by a good visit or by commercial pressure. A supplier whose questionnaire score falls below 62 is never approved, even if the visit goes well and even if the buyer has no alternative source. The reasoning is that a low score shows the supplier either lacks basic systems or would not be honest about them, and either problem outweighs anything a single visit can reveal. The supplier may reapply after six months with evidence of improvement.

Approved suppliers enter a review cycle. Every year their certificates are refreshed, their performance on deliveries and complaints is scored, and high-risk suppliers receive another visit. Any serious complaint or failed delivery check can trigger an early review. Suppliers who fall below standard are moved to conditional status, which limits what they can supply until the issue is resolved.

title: Batch traceability through the supply chain
note: Traceability is the ability to follow any ingredient forward into the finished products that contain it, and any finished product back to the batches of ingredients used. Brackenridge records batch codes at goods in, at weighing and at packing so that the chain is unbroken.

title: One step forward one step back traceability within four hours
note: For any batch, the plant must be able to identify the direct supplier lots used and the direct customers who received the finished product within four hours. The four hour target comes from regulator guidance and is tested during mock recalls.

title: Quarterly mock recall exercise
note: Each plant runs a mock recall every quarter. The compliance lead picks a finished batch without warning and the team must trace it fully within the four hour target. Results, gaps and timings are reported to the compliance committee. One exercise each year is run outside office hours.

title: Food safety incident reporting
note: A food safety incident is any event where unsafe or wrongly labelled food has left our control or is likely to have done so. Examples include a positive pathogen result on dispatched product, a missing allergen on a label, or foreign bodies found by a customer. Incidents must be reported to the regulator and handled through the recall procedure where needed.

title: Notify the regulator within 24 hours of a contamination incident
note: Once Brackenridge becomes aware that contaminated food may have reached customers, the regulator must be notified within 24 hours. The clock starts when any manager knows, not when the investigation is finished. Notification can be made by phone to the duty officer and confirmed in writing afterwards.

title: Delayed reporting due to weekend staffing
note: At weekends only a duty manager is on site, and they may not recognise that an event counts as a reportable incident. Calls to the technical manager sometimes go unanswered. This could cause us to miss the 24 hour notification window.

title: Product recall and withdrawal
note: A product recall removes unsafe food from customers and consumers. Brackenridge distinguishes a withdrawal, where product is recovered from the supply chain before consumers buy it, from a recall, where consumers are told to return or destroy it. Both are coordinated by an incident team led by the technical manager.

title: Recall contact tree
note: The recall contact tree lists who must be called, in what order, when a recall starts. It includes internal roles, the regulator duty line, the insurer, key retail customers and the logistics provider. The tree is tested during mock recalls and updated whenever someone changes role.

title: Recall execution playbook
note:
The recall execution playbook is the detailed guide the incident team follows once a decision has been made to withdraw or recall a Brackenridge product. It sits behind the shorter recall procedure and is written so that a capable person who has never run a recall could still follow it at three in the morning. It covers roles, communications, physical recovery of stock, regulator contact, and how the incident is closed.

The first hour is about stopping further harm. The technical manager confirms the affected product, batch codes and date range. Warehouse staff place an immediate hold on all matching stock still on site and in the third-party cold store. The logistics provider is asked to stop any deliveries in transit and return them. At the same time the incident team is assembled, usually the technical manager, the operations director, the commercial lead, the compliance lead and someone from customer service, with clear names written on the incident board against each role.

The second step is scoping the distribution. Using the traceability system, the compliance lead lists every customer who received affected stock, the quantity, the delivery date and the delivery point. For retail customers this often means hundreds of individual stores. The list is checked against the logistics provider's own delivery records because past exercises showed small discrepancies between our dispatch data and what was actually delivered.

The third step is regulator contact. The regulator is told what is known, what is being done and what is still uncertain. Drafts of the consumer notice and point-of-sale notice are shared for comment before they are published. The regulator may ask for changes in wording, and we generally accept them because a joint message travels further and attracts less criticism later.

The fourth step is customer notification. Most retail customers use a shared industry portal through which suppliers post withdrawal and recall notices, and their store systems then block the product at the till. Food service customers are contacted by phone and email by the commercial team using the recall contact tree. Every notification is logged with the time, the person contacted and the confirmation received. A customer is not considered notified until they have confirmed receipt.

Communications to the public are handled carefully. The consumer notice uses plain words, names the product, pack size, batch codes and dates exactly as printed, explains the risk without alarm, and tells people what to do. It is published on our website, shared with the regulator for their alert service and sent to any consumer media contacts the regulator recommends. Social media questions are answered with the same approved wording, and staff are reminded not to comment on the recall in a personal capacity. A single spokesperson, normally the operations director, handles any press calls, and every other person in the business refers questions to them rather than trying to help.

There is an important exception to portal notification. The Haverly Stores account must always be phoned directly, because their head office does not act on portal notices for suppliers of our size and will only accept a phone call to their product safety duty line, which is staffed until 22:00. If a recall starts later than that, the call is made at 06:00 the next morning and a written notice is emailed overnight so that it is waiting when their team arrives. This exception is written into our supply contract with them.

Recovery and reconciliation follow. Returned stock is counted, compared with the quantity dispatched and destroyed under supervision with a destruction certificate. The recovery rate is tracked daily. When the rate stops rising and the regulator agrees, the incident is closed. A review meeting is held within two weeks to capture lessons, and any changes to the playbook or contact tree are made before the next mock recall.

title: Microbiological sampling plan
note: The microbiological sampling plan sets out which finished products, ingredients and environmental surfaces are tested for bacteria, how often, and for which organisms. Sample sizes and frequencies are based on product risk and history. Results feed into release decisions and into trend reviews of hygiene performance.

title: Listeria swabs in high-care areas weekly
note: High-care areas, where cooked product is exposed before sealing, must be swabbed for listeria every week. Swab points include drains, floor junctions, the underside of conveyors and equipment frames. A positive result triggers intensified cleaning and a run of follow-up swabs until three consecutive negatives are achieved.

title: Use an external accredited lab for pathogen tests
note: We decided that all pathogen testing goes to an external accredited laboratory rather than our on-site lab. Culturing pathogens on site would create a contamination risk inside the factory and would need specialist containment we do not have. The on-site lab continues to run indicator organism tests and rapid protein swabs.

title: Positive listeria swab in drain
note: A positive listeria result in a high-care drain suggests a harbourage that could spread to product contact surfaces. Drains are hard to clean fully and can splash during washdown. If not controlled, this could lead to contaminated finished product and a recall.

title: Environmental monitoring of the factory
note: Environmental monitoring checks the cleanliness of the factory itself, not just the food. It combines microbiological swabs, air sampling in high-care rooms, visual inspections and protein tests. Results are plotted on site maps so recurring hotspots stand out.

title: Training and competence
note: Every person who handles food or makes food safety decisions must be trained and competent for their role. Training needs are defined in a matrix that links each job to required courses and assessments. Records show who has completed what and when refreshers are due.

title: Food handlers complete level two hygiene training before starting
note: New food handlers must complete level two food hygiene training before working unsupervised on any production line. Until then they work alongside a trained buddy and cannot sign any monitoring record.

title: Refresher training every two years
note: We decided that all food handlers repeat hygiene training every two years, more often than the code requires. Audit evidence showed that habits drift after about eighteen months, particularly hand washing and glove changes.

title: Training records and competency assessment
note:
This note explains how Brackenridge records training and checks that people are actually competent, not simply that they attended a course. Inspectors increasingly ask operators to explain a control in their own words, and a signed attendance sheet does not help if the person cannot do so. The approach therefore combines training records with practical observation.

The training matrix is the starting point. It lists every role in both plants against the food safety training that role needs, such as hygiene, allergen awareness, critical control point monitoring, cleaning chemicals and metal detector checks. Each cell shows whether the training is required before starting, within the first month, or at a set refresher interval. Supervisors can see their team's status on a dashboard, with overdue items shown first.

Training is delivered in three ways. Formal courses, such as level two hygiene, are run by accredited trainers and end with a written test. Task training is delivered on the line by a qualified trainer using the work instruction for that task. Toolbox talks are short sessions given at shift start, often after an audit finding or near miss, and they are recorded with attendance.

Competency assessment happens after task training. A qualified assessor observes the person doing the task on at least two separate shifts and asks a set of questions to check understanding. For critical control point monitoring the questions always include what the limit is, what to do if it is missed and who to tell. The person is only signed off as competent when both observations and the questions are satisfactory. Until then, their monitoring records must be countersigned.

Records are held in the training system, which is linked to the line terminals. A person whose required training or competency is not current cannot log in to record monitoring checks on that line. This hard link was introduced after an audit found a monitoring record signed by someone whose competency had lapsed months earlier.

Trainers themselves must be qualified. A line trainer needs at least a year in the role they train, a train-the-trainer course and a sign-off from the quality manager after delivering a session under observation. The quality manager keeps a list of approved trainers per line, and only people on that list can sign task training records. When a work instruction changes, every approved trainer for that line is briefed before the change goes live so that nobody trains the old method by habit. Training content is reviewed annually, and any audit finding that points to a knowledge gap results in a toolbox talk within the following week.

Temporary agency workers are a particular challenge, because they may work only a few shifts and often have limited English. They complete a short induction on arrival and receive a laminated pictorial card covering hand washing, protective clothing, allergen rules and how to report a problem. The card is printed in six languages, and only version seven or later of the card may be issued, because earlier versions showed an outdated glove-change rule. Gatehouse staff check the version number printed in the corner before handing cards out, and old cards are collected and shredded.

Refresher training is tracked automatically, and reminders go to supervisors two months before expiry. Competency is reassessed whenever a person moves to a new line, after a long absence, and whenever they are involved in a deviation. The training records themselves are kept for the duration of employment plus three years.

title: Pest control on site
note: Pest control keeps rodents, insects and birds out of production and storage areas. Brackenridge uses a contracted pest control service, bait stations mapped on a site plan, insect light traps and proofing of doors and drains. Activity trends are reviewed monthly.

title: Pest contractor visits eight times a year
note: The pest control contractor must carry out at least eight routine visits a year at each plant, plus call-outs within 24 hours when activity is reported. Each visit produces a report with findings and recommendations that the plant manager must acknowledge.

title: Bird ingress at loading bay
note: Birds have been seen inside the Pennick Moor loading bay when the dock doors are left open during deliveries. Droppings near raw material storage could contaminate packaging. Fast-acting doors are planned, but until then staff must close doors between vehicles.

title: Water quality in production
note: Water used as an ingredient or for cleaning food contact surfaces must be of drinking quality. Brackenridge takes mains water, tests it at outlets quarterly and keeps a map of every water outlet with its purpose. Hoses are stored off the floor and flushed before use.

title: Corrective and preventive actions
note: Corrective and preventive actions, often called CAPA, are the steps taken to fix a problem and stop it happening again. A correction removes the immediate issue, a corrective action addresses the cause, and a preventive action reduces the chance of similar problems elsewhere.

title: CAPA tracker register
note: The CAPA tracker is the shared register of every open corrective and preventive action, its source, owner, due date and evidence of closure. It is reviewed weekly by plant managers and quarterly by the compliance committee. Overdue items are highlighted automatically.

title: Root cause analysis using five whys for major findings
note: For every major or critical finding, the owner must complete a five whys analysis before proposing actions. This forces the team past the first obvious answer, which is often simply that someone made a mistake.

title: Should minor findings also need a root cause?
note: Minor findings currently need only a correction. Some managers argue that clusters of minor findings hide a bigger issue and should need a simple root cause statement too. Others worry about the extra paperwork for trivial items.

title: External inspection preparation
note:
This note describes how Brackenridge stays ready for inspections by the Northmere Food Standards Office and by retail customer auditors. Most regulator inspections are unannounced, so the guiding idea is that the plant should be inspection-ready every day rather than tidied up when a visit is expected. Preparation is therefore mostly about habits, with a short checklist for the first hour of a visit.

Daily readiness depends on the basics: clean and tidy production areas, complete monitoring records, functioning hand wash stations, labelled chemicals and no unexplained items in production rooms. Supervisors do a short walk at the start of each shift using a one page list, and anything that would embarrass us in front of an inspector is fixed before production starts. The walk takes ten minutes and is recorded.

Documentation readiness means that the core documents can be produced within minutes. These include the hazard analysis plans, the training matrix, the cleaning schedules, the pest control file, the latest internal audit reports and the open actions in the corrective action tracker. Each document has a named owner and a known location in the document vault, and the compliance lead checks a random selection each month to confirm they can be found quickly.

When an inspector arrives, the gatehouse calls the plant manager, the quality manager and the compliance lead. Whoever arrives first greets the inspector, confirms their identity and the purpose of the visit, and agrees a plan for the day. Production continues normally unless the inspector asks otherwise, because stopping lines can look like hiding something. A room is made available for document review, with network access to the vault.

During the inspection, answers are honest and direct. Staff are told that it is fine to say they do not know and will find out. Nobody guesses or speculates. Requests for documents are logged and fulfilled promptly. Any issue the inspector raises is noted in their words and, where it can be fixed immediately, it is fixed while they are still on site, with the fix shown to them before they leave.

Retail customer audits are different in tone but similar in practice. They are usually announced, follow a published standard and are run by an auditor who visits many suppliers. Before each one, the quality manager reviews the customer's standard for any clauses that go beyond the code, such as stricter glass policies or specific foreign body controls, and checks our evidence against them. Retail audit scores affect our ability to supply, so findings are treated with the same urgency as regulator findings. A shared calendar records all expected customer audits, and the plant manager is told at least a week ahead so that major maintenance work is not scheduled for that day.

There are two specific rules about escorting. Inspectors are always accompanied by someone who did not personally prepare or clean the area being inspected that day, so that the person answering questions is not defending their own work. The visitor log for inspectors is kept in a separate orange binder at the gatehouse rather than the general visitor book, so that inspection visits can be listed quickly when the annual return is prepared.

After the inspection a debrief is held the same day. Findings are entered into the corrective action tracker with owners and dates, and the formal report from the regulator is reviewed by the board within one month. Lessons from the visit are shared with the other plant so that both sites benefit.

title: Inspection reports reviewed by the board within one month
note: Every formal inspection report from the regulator must be presented to the board within one month of receipt, together with the action plan. The board minutes record whether the plan was accepted.

title: Labelling compliance on packs
note: Labelling compliance covers ingredient lists, allergen emphasis, nutrition panels, storage instructions, use-by dates and the business address. The technical team owns label content, while packing staff check that the correct label is on the correct product.

title: Use-by dates validated by shelf life study
note: Every use-by date printed on a Brackenridge product must be supported by a shelf life study showing the product stays safe until that date under the stated storage conditions. Studies are repeated when recipes or packaging change.

title: Extend soup shelf life from 10 to 12 days after challenge test
note: After a challenge test showed that spoilage organisms stayed within limits for 14 days, we decided to extend the use-by on standard soup pots from 10 to 12 days, keeping a two day safety margin. The extension does not apply to the one litre family pots.

title: Shelf life claims unsupported after recipe change
note: If a recipe is changed, for example by lowering salt, the original shelf life study may no longer apply. Without a new study the use-by date could be wrong, which the regulator treats as a serious labelling failure.

title: Change control for recipes
note: Change control ensures that recipe, process and packaging changes are assessed for food safety before they happen. Each change request describes what will change and why, and the technical team decides whether new studies, label updates or hazard analysis revisions are needed.

title: Recipe changes reviewed by the HACCP team before trial
note: No recipe change may go to a factory trial until the hazard analysis team has reviewed it and recorded their decision. Small kitchen trials are allowed, but nothing produced in them may be sold.

title: Confidential whistleblowing channel for staff
note: Staff can report food safety concerns confidentially through a phone line and web form run by an independent provider. Reports go to the operations director and the non-executive chair. Retaliation against anyone who raises a concern in good faith is a disciplinary offence.

title: Should we pursue the voluntary gold standard certification?
note: A voluntary industry certification scheme offers a gold grade that some retailers now prefer. It would need extra resources for documentation and an annual third-party audit. Is the commercial benefit worth the cost and effort?

title: Regulatory horizon scanning
note: Horizon scanning means watching for upcoming changes to the code, guidance notes and customer standards so that Brackenridge has time to prepare. The compliance lead reviews regulator bulletins monthly and summarises relevant changes for the committee.

title: Appoint a single compliance owner per plant
note: Each plant now has one named compliance owner who is accountable for its filings, audits and inspection readiness. Before this, responsibilities were split across several managers and deadlines were missed when people assumed someone else had them in hand.

title: Tallyport product overview
note: Tallyport is the field service scheduling and invoicing product built by Corvane Software. Office staff use the web app to schedule jobs and raise invoices, and technicians use the mobile app to see their day, record work, capture signatures and take payments. The delivery team is about forty engineers split into five squads.

title: Release train model for Tallyport
note: Tallyport ships on a release train: a fixed schedule where whatever is ready and tested boards the next release, and anything not ready waits for the following one. The train model replaced feature-based releases, which kept slipping because one large change would hold everything else back.

title: Ship releases every two weeks on Tuesday
note: Web releases go out every second Tuesday morning. Tuesday was chosen because Monday is the busiest scheduling day for customers and Friday leaves no time to react before the weekend. Hotfixes can ship on any working day with approval from the release manager.

title: Release checklist for Tallyport
note:
The release checklist is the shared list of steps that the release manager works through for every scheduled Tallyport release. It exists because releases involve many small actions spread across people and tools, and skipping any one of them has caused trouble in the past. The checklist lives in the release ticket template, and each item must be ticked with a name and time.

The checklist begins on the Thursday before release day with the code freeze. At freeze, the release branch is cut from main and only fixes approved by the release manager can be cherry-picked onto it. Squads are reminded the day before so that nobody is surprised. Feature work continues on main and simply catches the next train.

Between freeze and release, the quality team runs the regression suite against the release candidate on the staging environment. Automated tests cover the bulk of the product, while a short manual pass checks the areas automation handles poorly, such as printed invoice layout, signature capture on real devices and payment terminal pairing. Any failure is triaged within the day as either a release blocker, a known issue to document, or a test problem.

The checklist then covers database changes. Every migration in the release is listed with its expected run time on production-sized data, measured on the staging copy. Migrations expected to take more than a minute need an explicit plan, which usually means running them ahead of the release as a separate step during a quiet period. The on-call engineer for release day must confirm they have read the migration list.

Next comes communications. Support and customer success receive the draft release notes on the Friday, so they can prepare for questions. Any change that alters how customers work, such as a moved button or a new required field, gets an in-app message and a short article in the help centre. Customer-facing changelog entries are written in plain language and reviewed by someone outside engineering.

On release morning, the release manager confirms that the error rate and latency dashboards are healthy before starting, because releasing into an existing problem makes diagnosis harder. The deployment is rolled out to a canary group of internal and friendly customer accounts first. After thirty minutes with no new errors, the rollout continues to all customers in stages over the next hour, with automatic rollback if error rates rise above the threshold.

After the web rollout, the checklist moves to monitoring. The release manager watches dashboards for two hours, and the support lead reports any unusual tickets. Feature flags for features shipping dark are left off and are turned on separately later, so the release itself only changes code paths that are already expected.

Mobile releases follow the same checklist with some extra steps, because the app stores add their own review and rollout controls. The mobile build must be submitted for store review by the Friday before release day, and the web release is not held for the mobile one unless the two depend on each other. On Android the staged rollout always starts at 7 percent of users rather than the store default, then moves to 30 percent after a day and to everyone after three days if crash rates stay flat. The iPhone build uses phased release with the store's own schedule.

The final item on the checklist is a short retrospective note in the release ticket: what went well, what went wrong and whether any checklist item should be added, changed or removed. Proposed changes are reviewed monthly by the release managers.

title: Release 4.2 scope and freeze
note: Release 4.2 of Tallyport includes the new recurring job templates, faster schedule board loading and the first part of the invoice designer behind a flag. Code freeze for 4.2 is on the Thursday before release, and any item not merged by then moves to 4.3. The release manager for 4.2 publishes the final scope in the release channel at freeze.

title: Release slips due to late QA sign-off
note: When the regression suite finds problems late in the week, quality sign-off can slip past the Monday deadline, pushing the release. Repeated slips erode trust in the train and tempt squads to rush fixes onto the release branch.

title: Continuous integration pipeline
note: Every pull request to Tallyport runs through the continuous integration pipeline: lint, type checks, unit tests, integration tests against a disposable database, a security scan and a build of the web and mobile bundles. Merges to main are blocked unless every required job passes.

title: Main branch build under 15 minutes
note: The full CI pipeline on main must complete in under 15 minutes at the 90th percentile. Longer builds slow merges, encourage batching of unrelated changes and make it harder to find which change broke the build.

title: Flaky end-to-end tests
note: Some browser-based end-to-end tests fail intermittently because of timing, shared test data or third-party sandboxes. Engineers learn to rerun failures without reading them, which means real failures can be waved through.

title: Quarantine flaky tests automatically
note: Tests that fail and then pass on retry more than three times in a week are moved automatically to a quarantine suite that does not block merges. The owning squad gets a ticket and has two weeks to fix or delete the test.

title: CI feedback loop time
note: The CI feedback loop is the time between an engineer pushing a change and learning whether it passes. Short loops keep engineers focused on one change at a time. Tallyport tracks median and slow-end loop times per repository on the engineering dashboard.

title: CI infrastructure design
note:
This note describes the infrastructure that runs Tallyport's continuous integration jobs: where builds run, how capacity is managed, how caching works and how secrets are kept safe. It was written after a period of slow and unreliable builds, when engineers were waiting up to forty minutes for results on busy afternoons.

Builds run on a fleet of ephemeral runners. Each job gets a fresh virtual machine that is destroyed afterwards, so nothing from one build can leak into another. This costs a little start-up time but removed a whole class of problems where leftover files or processes from a previous job caused confusing failures. Runner images are rebuilt weekly with current operating system patches and toolchains.

Capacity is managed by an autoscaler that watches the job queue. When jobs are waiting, it starts more runners up to a maximum, and when runners are idle for ten minutes it shuts them down. The maximum exists to protect the budget, and it was set by looking at the busiest hour of a typical week and adding headroom. The autoscaler reports queue time as a metric, and alerts fire when the median wait exceeds two minutes.

Caching is the biggest single lever on build time. Dependency downloads are cached per lockfile hash so that unchanged dependencies are never fetched twice. Build outputs are stored in a remote cache keyed by the inputs of each build step, which means a test target whose code has not changed can reuse a previous result instead of running again. Cache hit rate is tracked per pipeline and usually sits above eighty percent.

Secrets used by CI, such as tokens for publishing packages and credentials for the test payment sandbox, are stored in a secrets manager and injected only into the jobs that need them. Jobs triggered from forks or untrusted branches never receive secrets. Every use of a secret is logged, and secrets are rotated every ninety days or immediately if a log shows unexpected use.

Test databases are created per job from a template snapshot, which takes a few seconds instead of running all migrations from scratch. The snapshot is refreshed nightly from the latest main branch so that it stays close to the current schema.

Observability for CI itself was added later than it should have been. Every job now emits timings for each step, cache results and the runner type used. These feed a dashboard that shows which steps are slowest and which tests fail most often, and it is reviewed in the monthly developer experience meeting.

The fleet scales between a floor of 6 and a ceiling of 48 Linux runners. Mobile builds need macOS machines, which cannot be created on demand in the same way, so the team leases a fixed pool of eight dedicated macOS runners from a single supplier, Lindqvist Hosting, on a yearly contract. Because there is only one supplier, an outage on their side stops all iPhone builds, and the team keeps a written fallback of building on two office machines in an emergency.

Cost is reviewed every quarter. The largest items are runner compute time, cache storage and the leased machines described above. Engineers can see the cost of their own pipelines on the dashboard, which has encouraged several squads to trim slow and redundant jobs without being asked.

Changes to the CI infrastructure are made through the same review process as product code, using configuration stored in the repository, so every change has an author, a reviewer and a history.

title: Shared build cache component
note: The build cache stores outputs of build steps keyed by their inputs, so unchanged parts of the codebase are not rebuilt or retested. It is shared between CI and developer laptops, which also speeds up local builds after pulling main.

title: Remote build cache shared across branches
note: We decided that the remote cache is readable by every branch but writable only by builds on main. This lets feature branches reuse main's results while preventing an untrusted branch from poisoning the cache.

title: Feature flags in Tallyport
note: Feature flags let the team ship code that is turned off by default and enable it later for some or all customers without a new deploy. Tallyport uses flags for gradual rollouts, beta programmes and emergency kill switches on risky features.

title: Feature flag cleanup
note: Feature flag cleanup is the routine removal of flags, and the code behind the dead branch, once a feature is fully rolled out or abandoned. A small script lists flags that have been fully on or fully off for more than a month and opens tickets for the owning squad.

title: Flags removed within 60 days after full rollout
note: Once a feature flag has been enabled for all customers, the flag and the old code path must be removed within 60 days. Kill switches meant to stay permanently must be registered as such and are exempt.

title: Stale flags creating untested code paths
note: Every flag doubles the number of possible behaviours in the code it guards. Old flags that nobody remembers can be flipped by accident, sending customers down a path that has not been tested in months.

title: Percentage rollouts for billing changes
note: Any change that affects how invoices are calculated or sent must be released behind a flag and rolled out by percentage of accounts, starting at one percent. Billing mistakes are costly to unwind, so a slow rollout limits the damage if something is wrong.

title: Incident management process
note: Incident management is how the team responds when Tallyport is down or badly degraded. An incident commander coordinates, a communications lead updates the status page and support, and engineers investigate and mitigate. Severity levels decide who is paged and how often updates are posted.

title: Incident postmortem for the 14 March sync outage
note:
On 14 March the Tallyport mobile sync service stopped accepting updates from technicians for just under three hours during the busiest part of the morning. Technicians could still see their schedules from cache, but job updates, photos and signatures queued on their phones and did not reach the office. This postmortem records what happened, why, and what we are changing. It follows our blameless format.

The first signal was a rise in sync errors reported by the mobile app telemetry at 07:42. The alert threshold was set for a sustained error rate over five minutes, so the page did not fire until 07:51. The on-call engineer acknowledged within four minutes and initially suspected the mobile release from the previous evening, because it had changed how retries were scheduled. This was a reasonable first guess but turned out to be wrong, and it cost about forty minutes.

At 08:30 an incident commander was assigned and the incident was raised to the highest severity because offices began calling support in large numbers. The communications lead posted the first status page update at 08:38, nearly an hour after the problem began. Customers told us afterwards that this delay was the most frustrating part of the morning, because they could not tell their technicians whether to keep working or to switch to paper.

Rolling back the mobile release did not help, and by 09:10 the team had moved on to the sync service itself. Its dashboards showed normal processor and memory use, but request latency was extremely high and the number of open database connections was flat at a suspicious round number. Engineers noticed that requests were waiting for a connection rather than doing work.

The mitigation at 10:31 was to raise the connection limit and restart the service instances one at a time. Queued updates from phones began to drain within minutes, and by 10:40 the backlog was cleared. No data was lost, because the mobile app had kept everything locally and retried as designed. Some technicians had duplicated work on paper, which offices had to reconcile by hand.

During the incident, support received more than three hundred calls. The support lead set up a shared message for agents within the first hour, but agents had no reliable estimate of recovery time to give customers, and several customers told us they had been given conflicting answers by different agents. This is captured as a separate action for the support playbook rather than an engineering fix.

The investigation then asked why the connection limit was so low. A configuration change two weeks earlier had moved the sync service onto a new deployment template. The template's connection pool settings had been taken from another service where they made sense, and nobody reviewing the change noticed that the sync service needs many more concurrent connections at peak.

The root cause was that the sync service's database connection pool was capped at 200, a value copied from staging configuration where traffic is a tiny fraction of production. On a normal day this limit was close to the peak but not over it. On 14 March a large customer added two hundred new technicians who all synced for the first time that morning, pushing demand past the cap.

Actions agreed: connection pool limits are now set per environment and reviewed as part of the service template; an alert fires when pool usage exceeds eighty percent for five minutes; the first status page update must go out within fifteen minutes of a highest-severity page; and the on-call runbook now asks engineers to check resource saturation before suspecting a recent release.

title: Postmortems published within five working days
note: Every highest and second-highest severity incident must have a written postmortem published to the engineering wiki within five working days. Customer-facing summaries are prepared by support from the same document.

title: Blameless postmortem format
note: Postmortems describe what the system and the process allowed to happen, not who made a mistake. Names appear only for roles in the timeline. The aim is for people to share honestly what they saw and did, which they will not do if they expect blame.

title: On-call rotation structure
note: Engineers join the on-call rotation after three months on the team. Each shift lasts a week, with a primary and a secondary engineer. On-call engineers are paid a weekly allowance plus time off in lieu for any night pages.

title: On-call escalation policy
note: The on-call escalation policy defines who gets paged next if an alert is not acknowledged. The primary engineer is paged first, the secondary after ten minutes, and the engineering manager on duty after twenty. Highest-severity incidents page the incident commander rota at the same time as the primary.

title: Pager acknowledged within 10 minutes
note: The primary on-call engineer must acknowledge a page within 10 minutes, day or night. Acknowledging means they are looking at the problem, not that it is fixed. Missed acknowledgements are reviewed without blame to see if the rota or alert routing needs to change.

title: On-call fatigue among engineers
note: A few noisy services generate most night pages, and the same senior engineers often get pulled into incidents even when not on call. Over time this leads to tiredness, mistakes and people leaving the team.

title: Split rotation between two time zones
note: Once the second engineering office opened, we split on-call so that each office covers its own daytime hours and nobody is paged at night except for the highest severity. Handover happens at a fixed time with a short written note.

title: Database migrations during deploys
note: Database migrations are scripted changes to the structure of Tallyport's production database, such as adding a column, creating an index or splitting a table. They run automatically during deploys and are written so that the old and new versions of the application can both run against the database during a rollout.

title: Primary database to sharded cluster migration plan
note:
This plan describes how Tallyport will move from a single large primary database to a cluster where customer accounts are spread across several shards. The single primary has served the product well, but growth means it now runs close to its limits on write throughput at month end, and every large customer that joins makes the problem worse. The goal of the migration is to remove that ceiling without customer-visible downtime.

The chosen design splits data by tenant. Every customer account, called a tenant in the code, lives entirely on one shard, along with all its jobs, invoices, technicians and attachments metadata. A small directory service records which shard each tenant lives on, and the application looks up the shard at the start of each request. Data shared across tenants, such as reference tables of tax rates, is copied to every shard.

Before any data moves, the application must be made shard-aware. This means removing the handful of queries that join across tenants, mostly in internal reporting, and routing every database call through a connection layer that knows which shard to use. This work is happening now behind a flag, with the directory pointing every tenant at the existing primary, so the code paths can be tested in production long before any data moves.

Data moves tenant by tenant. For each tenant, the migration tool copies the existing rows to the target shard, then streams ongoing changes from the primary until the copy is caught up. At that point writes for the tenant are paused for a few seconds, the last changes are applied, the directory is updated and writes resume against the new shard. The pause is short enough that the mobile app's retry logic hides it from technicians.

Tenants are grouped into batches by size and risk. Small internal and test accounts go first, followed by small paying customers who have agreed to be early movers, then medium customers, and finally the largest accounts. Each batch is followed by a soak period of at least a week, during which the team watches error rates, query latency and support tickets for the moved tenants before starting the next batch.

Rollback is possible at any stage. The primary keeps receiving a stream of changes from the shard for each moved tenant until the soak period ends, so a tenant can be pointed back at the primary quickly if something goes wrong. Only after the soak is complete is the tenant's data removed from the primary.

Risks include subtle bugs in queries that assumed a single database, increased operational complexity from running many databases instead of one, and the cost of more servers. The team is mitigating these with extensive testing on a production copy and by building tooling for common shard operations before they are needed.

The last batch contains the five largest tenants, which together account for nearly a third of all writes. Their cutover is scheduled in a single window from 02:00 to 04:30 on a Sunday morning, when job activity is lowest, with the full migration team online and customer success having warned each account a fortnight in advance. If any of the five fails to cut over within the window, the remaining ones are postponed to the following Sunday.

After the final batch, the old primary is kept read-only for a month for safety and then retired.

title: Migrations backward compatible for one release
note: Every schema change must work with both the current and the previous version of the application, because during a rollout both versions run at once and a rollback may be needed. Destructive changes such as dropping a column wait at least one release.

title: Expand and contract pattern for schema changes
note: Schema changes use the expand and contract pattern. First add the new structure and write to both old and new, then move reads to the new structure, and only later remove the old one. Each step is its own release.

title: Long-running migration locking the jobs table
note: The jobs table is the largest and busiest table. A migration that rewrites it or builds an index the wrong way can lock it for minutes, which stops scheduling for every customer. Such migrations must be run online with tools that avoid long locks.

title: Dependency management for third-party libraries
note: Dependency management covers the third-party libraries Tallyport relies on: choosing them, pinning versions in lockfiles, keeping them up to date, and checking licences and known vulnerabilities. Each dependency has an owning squad responsible for upgrades.

title: Dependency exemption list for licence scanning
note: The licence scanner blocks any dependency whose licence is not on the approved list. Some libraries have unusual licences that legal has reviewed and accepted case by case. These are recorded on an exemption list in the repository with the reviewer's name and the date of the decision.

title: Automated weekly dependency upgrade pull requests
note: A bot opens pull requests every Monday for available dependency upgrades, grouped by risk. Patch upgrades with passing CI are merged automatically. Minor and major upgrades need a human review by the owning squad.

title: Abandoned upstream date library
note: The date and time zone library used throughout the scheduling code has had no maintainer activity for over a year. If a serious bug or vulnerability appears, nobody upstream will fix it, and replacing it would touch hundreds of files.

title: Should we vendor the PDF rendering library?
note: Invoice PDFs depend on a rendering library that has broken our layout twice in minor upgrades. Copying a fixed version into our repository would stop surprise changes but means we must apply security fixes ourselves. Which cost is lower?

title: Mobile sync engine
note: The sync engine moves data between the mobile app and the server. It keeps a local database on the phone, records every change as an operation, and sends operations to the server when there is a connection. The server merges operations from many devices and sends back updates.

title: Sync engine prototype spike
note: A two week spike built a throwaway prototype of a new sync engine based on per-field change tracking instead of whole-record updates. The prototype was not production code. It was used to measure data volume, battery use and merge behaviour on real devices before deciding whether to rebuild the engine.

title: Offline sync design for the mobile app
note:
Technicians often work in basements, plant rooms and rural sites with no signal, so the Tallyport mobile app must work fully offline and catch up later. This design note explains how the app stores data, records changes, resolves conflicts and recovers from failures. It reflects the current engine and the lessons from the recent prototype work.

The app holds a local database containing the technician's jobs for the next seven days, the customer and site details for those jobs, price lists, forms and any attachments already downloaded. Data outside that window is fetched on demand when there is a connection. Keeping the local set small keeps the app fast and limits what is exposed if a phone is lost.

Every change made on the device is recorded as an operation in an outbox: set a field, add a line item, attach a photo, capture a signature. Operations have an identifier, the time on the device, and the version of the record they were based on. When a connection is available, the outbox is sent in order. The server acknowledges each operation, and acknowledged operations are removed from the outbox.

Photos and signatures are large, so they are uploaded separately from the operations that reference them. An operation that refers to a photo not yet uploaded is held on the server until the photo arrives. This prevents an invoice being raised with a missing signature image.

Conflicts happen when the office and the technician change the same record while the technician is offline. Most conflicts are on different fields and merge without trouble, because the server applies changes field by field. When both sides change the same field, the server needs a rule to decide which change wins.

Clock skew on phones makes timestamps unreliable for deciding which change came first. The server therefore uses the record version the device was based on, not the device clock. If the device edited an outdated version, the server knows a conflict has occurred and applies the field rules.
