Failures are expected. If the app crashes mid-sync, the outbox is still intact on restart and the server ignores duplicates by identifier. If the server rejects an operation as invalid, the app shows the technician a clear message on the affected job rather than silently dropping it. Support can see each device's outbox state from an admin page.

Deleted records need special care. If the office cancels a job while a technician is offline and the technician then completes it, the server does not silently discard the completion. Instead it reopens the job in a flagged state and alerts the office, because real work was done on site and the customer may need to be invoiced or contacted.

The field rules were agreed with product and customer advisers and are deliberately simple. For signatures, completion notes and photos, the technician's edit always wins, because the technician was physically present and the office cannot know better. For prices, discounts and line item rates, the office's edit always wins, because pricing is controlled centrally and technicians are not allowed to override it in the field. For all other fields the most recent server-side version wins and the losing value is kept in the record history so nobody's work is lost without trace.

Testing uses a simulator that runs hundreds of virtual devices against a test server with random disconnections. Every release of the sync code must pass a night of simulator runs with no lost or duplicated operations.

title: Observability of production services
note: Observability is the ability to understand what Tallyport is doing in production from the outside. The team uses structured logs, metrics, traces across services and real user monitoring in the web and mobile apps. Every service must expose health and saturation metrics.

title: Service level objectives
note: Service level objectives set target reliability for the most important user journeys, such as loading the schedule, syncing a job and sending an invoice. Each objective has a measurement, a target and a monthly error budget.

title: API availability 99.9 percent monthly
note: The public API must be available 99.9 percent of the time in each calendar month, measured by successful responses to synthetic checks from three regions. This target is published to customers on the trust page.

title: Error budget freezes feature work
note: If a service uses its full monthly error budget, its owning squad pauses feature work and spends the rest of the month on reliability. The rule turns reliability from a debate into an agreed trigger.

title: Alert noise hides real problems
note: Many alerts fire for conditions that fix themselves or need no action. Engineers start ignoring them, and a real problem can sit unnoticed among dozens of noisy notifications.

title: Two week sprint cadence
note: Engineering squads plan work in two week sprints aligned with the release train. Each sprint starts with planning on a Wednesday and ends with a review and retrospective. Unfinished work rolls over only after an explicit decision in planning.

title: Weekly backlog grooming sessions
note: Each squad spends an hour a week refining its backlog: splitting large tickets, clarifying acceptance criteria and estimating effort. Product managers bring customer evidence for new items so priorities rest on more than opinion.

title: Should QA be embedded in squads?
note: Quality engineers currently sit in a central team and test every squad's work before release. Embedding one in each squad might catch issues earlier, but could leave gaps when someone is away and weaken shared test tooling.

title: Shared staging environment
note: Staging is a full copy of the production stack used for release testing. It runs the release candidate against anonymised production-shaped data and connects to sandbox versions of payment and email providers.

title: Staging data drifts from production
note: Staging data is refreshed only monthly, so new customer configurations seen in production may be missing from staging. Bugs that depend on those configurations pass release testing and appear only after release.

title: Environment strategy from laptop to production
note:
This note sets out the environments Tallyport uses between a developer's laptop and production, what each one is for, who owns it and how data gets into it. Over the years the number of environments grew without a plan, and several were half-maintained copies that nobody trusted. The strategy reduces them to a small set with clear purposes.

Local development runs on the developer's machine using containers for the database, queue and search services. A seed script creates a realistic set of test accounts, jobs and invoices. Developers can point their local web app at a shared mock of the payment provider so they never need real payment credentials.

Preview environments are created automatically for every pull request that changes the web app. Each preview runs the branch's code against its own small database seeded with the same test data as local development. Product managers, designers and support staff use previews to try changes before they are merged, and the link is posted on the pull request.

Staging is the single shared pre-production environment. It runs the release candidate during the release week and main at other times. Its data is an anonymised copy of production, refreshed monthly, with names, addresses, phone numbers and emails replaced. Payment and email providers are pointed at sandbox accounts so nothing can reach a real customer.

Production is split by region, with a primary region for most customers and a second region for customers who need data to stay in that jurisdiction. Each region has its own database and storage, and deployments roll through regions one at a time.

Ownership is explicit. The platform squad owns the environment tooling and staging. Each product squad owns the correctness of its own services in every environment. The release manager has the final say over what runs on staging during release week.

Access to production data is tightly limited. Engineers do not have standing access, and requests for temporary access are approved per incident and logged. Staging data is anonymised precisely so that most investigations can happen there without touching production.

Configuration differences between environments are kept to a minimum and listed in a single file per service. Anything that differs, such as connection pool sizes, external service addresses or rate limits, must be named in that file with a short reason. This rule was added after an incident where a value copied from one environment to another went unnoticed for weeks. Reviewers are asked to look at this file first when a change touches more than one environment.

Costs are tracked per environment type. Preview environments turned out to be the fastest growing cost, because many were left running long after their pull request was merged or closed. Two rules now apply. A preview environment is shut down as soon as its pull request is merged or closed. Any preview still running after 72 hours is deleted automatically unless someone has added the label keep to the pull request, and even labelled previews are removed after two weeks. A weekly report lists the most expensive previews and their owners.

Changes to this strategy are proposed through the architecture review meeting and recorded in the decisions log. Any squad that wants an extra long-lived environment must explain why previews or staging cannot meet the need, name an owner, and agree a date when the environment will be reviewed or removed.

title: Code review practice
note: Every change to Tallyport is reviewed by at least one engineer other than the author before merging. Reviewers check correctness, tests, readability and risk. Small pull requests are encouraged because they get faster and better reviews.

title: Two approvals for billing code
note: Changes to code under the billing and payments directories need approval from two engineers, at least one of whom is in the billing squad. Ownership rules in the repository enforce this automatically.

title: Trunk based development
note: Engineers work on short-lived branches merged into main at least daily. Long-lived feature branches are not allowed. Incomplete features are hidden behind flags rather than kept off main.

title: Security patching routine
note: Security patching covers operating system updates on servers, upgrades to vulnerable libraries and fixes to vulnerabilities found in our own code. A weekly scan reports known vulnerabilities across all services, ranked by severity and exposure.

title: Critical vulnerabilities patched within 7 days
note: Vulnerabilities rated critical in any internet-facing service must be patched or mitigated within 7 days of discovery. High severity issues have 30 days. Exceptions need sign-off from the security lead.

title: Secrets committed to repository
note: Engineers occasionally paste credentials into configuration files while debugging and commit them by mistake. Even if removed later, the secret stays in history and must be treated as exposed.

title: Secret scanning in pre-commit hooks
note: A pre-commit hook scans staged changes for patterns that look like credentials and blocks the commit if one is found. The same scan runs in CI as a backstop for anyone who skips local hooks.

title: Mobile app delivery
note: The technician app is built from a single codebase for both phone platforms. Builds are produced in CI, distributed to internal testers through beta channels and then submitted to the app stores. Mobile releases follow the web release train but can lag by a few days.

title: App store review delays hotfix
note: An urgent fix for the mobile app cannot reach users until it passes store review, which can take anywhere from hours to several days. During that time technicians remain on the broken version.

title: Public API versioning scheme
note: Tallyport's public API is versioned by date in the request header. Customers pin to a version and upgrade when ready. Breaking changes only appear in new versions, while older versions keep working until they are retired.

title: Public API deprecation policy
note:
This policy explains how Corvane retires old versions and endpoints of the Tallyport public API. Customers build integrations with accounting systems, payroll tools and their own dashboards on top of the API, and those integrations are often maintained by small teams or outside contractors who cannot react quickly. The policy aims to give them plenty of warning and a clear path forward while letting the team stop maintaining old code.

An endpoint or version is deprecated when a better replacement exists and has been stable for at least one release cycle. Deprecation is a promise of future removal, not a removal. Deprecated endpoints continue to work exactly as before until their shutdown date.

When something is deprecated, three things happen at once. The API reference marks it clearly with the shutdown date and a link to the migration guide. The changelog announces it. And every account that has called the endpoint in the past ninety days receives an email to its technical contacts explaining what is changing and why.

The migration guide is written before the deprecation is announced, not after. It shows side by side examples of old and new calls, lists any differences in behaviour, and points out common mistakes. Support is briefed on the guide so they can answer questions.

During the deprecation window, the team monitors usage of the deprecated endpoint by account. Accounts still calling it are contacted again at the halfway point and one month before shutdown. Customer success managers are given a list of their accounts that are still affected so they can raise it during regular calls.

For large customers with complex integrations, the team may offer a short extension or a call with an engineer. Extensions are granted per account rather than by delaying the shutdown for everyone, and they are recorded so that the extended accounts receive their own reminders.

Brownouts are used before the final shutdown. For a few short scheduled periods in the last month, the deprecated endpoint returns an error explaining that it is deprecated. This catches integrations whose owners have ignored emails, because the failure appears in their own logs and monitoring.

Client libraries published by Corvane are updated alongside every deprecation. New library versions log a warning the first time a deprecated call is made, and the library release notes repeat the shutdown date. Libraries for older language versions are kept in step for as long as the endpoints they wrap are supported, so customers are never forced to upgrade their language runtime just to keep calling the API.

Responses from deprecated endpoints carry a sunset header giving the shutdown date in machine-readable form, so client libraries and monitoring can warn developers automatically. There is also a firm calendar rule: a final shutdown is never scheduled in December, because many customers freeze changes over their year-end and accounting integrations are under the most strain then. If the standard window would end in December, the shutdown moves to the second week of January.

After shutdown, calls to the removed endpoint return a clear error with a link to the migration guide for at least a year, rather than a generic not-found response. The policy itself is reviewed once a year by the API product manager, and any change to it is announced in the changelog with at least three months of notice before it takes effect.

title: Twelve month deprecation window
note: Deprecated API versions keep working for twelve months after the deprecation announcement. Shorter windows were rejected because customer integrations are often maintained by contractors who are engaged only once or twice a year.

title: Web performance budget
note: A performance budget sets limits on page weight, script size and load time for the key screens of the web app. Pull requests that push a screen over budget fail a CI check and need explicit approval from the web platform owner.

title: Schedule page loads under two seconds on mid-range phones
note: The technician's daily schedule must become usable within two seconds on a mid-range phone over a typical mobile connection. This is measured with real user monitoring, not only in the lab.

title: Production data backups
note: Production databases are backed up continuously with point-in-time recovery, and file storage for attachments is replicated to a second region. Backups are encrypted and kept for thirty-five days.

title: Restore test every quarter
note: Once a quarter the platform squad restores a full production backup into an isolated environment and checks that the application runs against it. The time taken is recorded and compared with the recovery target.

title: Backup restore never actually tested for attachments
note: Quarterly restore tests cover the database but have never restored attachment storage at full scale. If storage were lost, we do not know how long recovery of millions of photos and signatures would take.

title: Tech debt register
note: The tech debt register lists known shortcuts and weaknesses in the codebase, with an estimate of their cost and risk. Squads add items when they knowingly take a shortcut, and the register is reviewed each quarter to choose what to pay down.

title: Reserve 20 percent of sprint capacity for tech debt
note: Each squad reserves about a fifth of every sprint for items from the tech debt register or for reliability work. The reservation protects maintenance from being squeezed out by feature requests.

title: Should we split the monolith billing module?
note: Billing code sits inside the main application and is touched by many squads. Splitting it into a separate service could give clearer ownership and safer releases, but would add network calls and operational overhead. Is now the right time?

title: Internal release notes
note: Release notes describe what changed in each release for internal teams. They are generated from merged pull request titles and then edited by the release manager to group related changes and remove noise.

title: Public customer-facing changelog
note: The customer changelog is a public page listing new features, improvements and fixes in plain language. It is updated on release day and linked from the in-app help menu. Internal technical detail is left out.

title: Dark launch for the new invoice designer
note: The new invoice designer will ship to production turned off, then be enabled first for internal accounts and a small beta group. This dark launch lets us test it on real infrastructure without exposing customers who did not opt in.

title: Wrenfold Studio workshop practice
note: Wrenfold Studio is a small design consultancy that runs hands-on workshops for client organisations, mostly councils, charities and mid-sized service businesses. A typical engagement mixes discovery workshops, user research, prototyping and a final readout. The studio has six designers and two researchers, and every workshop has a lead facilitator and a supporting facilitator.

title: Workshop agenda design
note: Every workshop agenda is built backwards from the outputs the client needs by the end of the day. Each session has a stated purpose, a time box, a method and a named output. Agendas alternate between divergent activities that generate ideas and convergent ones that choose between them, with energy dips after lunch planned for.

title: Facilitation guide for discovery workshops
note:
This guide is for anyone at Wrenfold leading a discovery workshop, the first full-day session of most client engagements. Discovery workshops bring together client staff from different teams to build a shared picture of the problem, surface what people already know and agree which questions research should answer. They set the tone for the whole engagement, so the studio treats their facilitation as a craft.

Preparation starts two weeks before the day. The lead facilitator interviews the client sponsor about goals, politics and any topics that are off limits, and reads whatever the client has already written about the problem. A short pre-workshop survey goes to every participant asking what they hope to get out of the day and what they are worried about. Answers shape the agenda and help the facilitators spot tensions before they surface in the room.

The room matters. Participants sit at small tables of four to six, mixed across teams and seniority so that no table becomes a department meeting. Walls are cleared for large sheets. Phones and laptops are put away except during planned breaks, which is explained at the start as a request rather than a rule.

The day opens with a clear framing: why everyone is here, what the day will produce, what it will not decide, and how decisions made today will be used. The sponsor gives this framing in their own words, briefly, and then hands over to the facilitator. Ground rules are short and agreed by the group rather than imposed.

The morning is divergent. Participants map what they know about the people the service is for, the current journey, pain points and existing data. Methods include silent writing on sticky notes, sharing in pairs and then whole-table discussion. The facilitator's job is to keep things moving, make sure quiet people are heard and stop anyone from closing down ideas too early.

The afternoon is convergent. Groups cluster their notes, name themes and turn the most important unknowns into research questions. Each table presents back briefly, and the whole room votes on which questions matter most. The facilitator watches for false consensus, where people agree because they are tired or because a senior person has spoken.

Difficult moments are expected. A participant may dominate, challenge the purpose of the day or raise a grievance unrelated to the topic. The facilitator acknowledges the point, decides whether it belongs in the session, and if not records it visibly for later so the person knows it has been heard. The supporting facilitator watches the room and quietly tells the lead when someone looks lost or unhappy.

Timekeeping uses a few studio habits that clients often remember. Off-topic points go onto a parking board in the corner. Each session's remaining time is shown on a visible countdown. And at the three-hour mark the lead facilitator rings a small brass bell, which signals a compulsory ten minute break away from the room for everyone, including the facilitators and the sponsor. The bell started as a joke and stayed because it works: nobody argues with a bell.

The day closes by reading back the agreed research questions, confirming what happens next and thanking people by name for specific contributions. Within two working days the facilitators send a written summary with photographs of the key boards, so that participants can see their work was captured faithfully.

title: Cap workshops at twelve participants
note: Wrenfold limits in-person workshops to twelve participants plus two facilitators. Larger groups split into too many tables to manage, and the report-back sessions drag. If a client wants more people involved, we run two sessions rather than one big one.

title: Dominant voices in workshops
note: In many client rooms one or two senior or confident people speak most of the time, and others defer to them. Their views end up over-represented in the outputs, while front-line knowledge goes unheard.

title: Personas built from research
note: Personas are short descriptions of archetypal users built from research, each with goals, frustrations, context and behaviours. They help a team keep real people in mind when making design choices. Wrenfold's personas avoid stock photos and invented hobbies, focusing on what affects use of the service.

title: Proto-personas before research
note: At the start of an engagement, clients sketch proto-personas from what they already believe about their users. These are clearly labelled as assumptions and are tested and replaced once research is done. Making assumptions visible early makes them easier to challenge later.

title: Personas based on assumptions
note: If proto-personas are never replaced with research-based ones, teams end up designing for stereotypes. Clients sometimes like the early versions so much that they print them as posters before any evidence exists.

title: Journey maps for services
note: A journey map shows the steps a person goes through to achieve a goal with a service, along with what they do, think and feel at each step. It highlights pain points and moments that matter. Wrenfold builds journey maps from research rather than from internal process diagrams.

title: Journey map template
note: The studio's journey map template is a long horizontal sheet with lanes for stages, actions, touchpoints, thoughts, feelings, pain points and opportunities. A digital version exists for remote sessions. Facilitators are encouraged to remove lanes that do not suit a particular project.

title: Journey mapping method for service redesign
note:
This method note explains how Wrenfold runs journey mapping when a client is redesigning an existing service, such as a council's bulky waste collection or a charity's helpline. Mapping a service that already exists is different from imagining a new one, because there is real behaviour to observe, real complaints to read and real staff who know where things break.

The work starts with evidence gathering. Researchers observe the service in use, interview recent users and front-line staff, and read a sample of complaints and compliments. They also collect artefacts: letters, forms, web pages, text messages and scripts used by call handlers. Each artefact is printed and later pinned to the map at the step where people meet it.

Next, the team drafts the backbone of the journey: the main stages from the moment someone realises they need the service until they no longer think about it. Stages are named in the user's language, not the organisation's. For a waste collection that might mean stages such as noticing the old sofa needs to go, finding out how, booking, waiting, collection day and afterwards, rather than the council's internal terms.

The mapping workshop brings client staff and, where possible, a few users together. Participants work along the backbone, adding what the person does, what they see, what they think and where they get stuck at each stage. Evidence cards from the research are placed next to claims, so that a statement like people find booking easy can be checked against quotes and data.

Behind the user's experience, a second set of lanes shows what the organisation does at each step: which team acts, which system is used and where handoffs happen. Many pain points turn out to sit at handoffs between teams, where information is lost or someone waits for an answer that nobody owns.

Feelings are recorded in a dedicated lane. Rather than words alone, the studio uses a simple drawn scale so that highs and lows can be seen at a glance from across the room. Participants place each feeling based on evidence, and disagreements are discussed openly, because different users often feel very differently about the same step.

Opportunities are added last. For each pain point, participants write possible improvements, ranging from small fixes such as rewording a letter to larger changes such as merging two teams. Opportunities are not judged during mapping, only captured.

Mapping sessions with users present need extra care. Users are paid for their time, are never asked to defend their feelings against staff views, and sit at a table with a researcher rather than among managers. Their contributions are marked on the map with a distinct colour so their voice is visible.

The emotion lane uses a five-point scale drawn as simple faces, from very unhappy to very happy, with each step marked at one level. Once the map is complete, the lowest point on the entire journey is always marked with a single red dot sticker, and that step becomes the first candidate for prioritisation, before any voting happens. The studio adopted this rule after noticing that groups tend to vote for fixes they find interesting rather than for the moment that hurts users most.

The finished map is photographed, redrawn digitally and shared with the client as a living document, with a version number and a list of open questions. It is revisited at the end of the engagement to show which pain points were addressed. Clients are encouraged to keep a printed copy on a wall where staff walk past it, because a map hidden in a shared folder is soon forgotten.

title: Paper prototype session
note: In a paper prototype session, participants sketch screens or forms on paper and test them with each other or with real users, swapping pieces of paper as the user taps or moves on. Paper is quick to change and signals clearly that nothing is finished, which makes people more willing to criticise.

title: Clickable prototypes in design tools
note: Once an idea has survived paper testing, the studio builds a clickable prototype in a design tool, linking screens so that a user can move through a realistic flow. Clickable prototypes test layout, wording and sequence, but not real data or performance.

title: Low fidelity first rule
note: The studio's rule is that the first version of any idea shown to users must be low fidelity: paper, a whiteboard sketch or a plain grey wireframe. Polished visuals too early make people comment on colours rather than on whether the idea works.

title: Clients treat prototypes as finished designs
note: Client stakeholders sometimes see a convincing prototype and assume the product is nearly built. They then expect launch dates far sooner than development can deliver and are disappointed when the real build takes months.

title: Internal design critique sessions
note: A design critique is a structured session where designers show work in progress and colleagues give feedback against the goals of the work. Critique is about improving the design, not judging the designer. Wrenfold holds internal critiques twice a week.

title: Critiques start with stated goals
note: Every critique begins with the presenter stating what the design is trying to achieve, who it is for and what kind of feedback they want. Feedback that does not relate to those goals is noted but not discussed in the session.

title: Silent critique round before discussion
note: Before anyone speaks, reviewers spend five minutes writing their own feedback on notes. This stops the first speaker from setting the direction for everyone else and makes sure quieter reviewers contribute.

title: Critique protocol for design reviews
note:
The critique protocol sets out exactly how Wrenfold runs design critiques, both internally and with clients. It exists because unstructured feedback sessions tend to drift into personal taste, rewards confident speakers and leaves presenters feeling attacked or confused about what to do next. A good critique should leave the presenter with clearer thinking and a short list of changes worth trying.

Critiques are booked in advance with a fixed length, usually forty-five minutes, and a maximum of six reviewers. The presenter shares the work beforehand when possible, along with a short note covering the goal, the audience, the constraints and the specific questions they want answered. Reviewers are expected to read this before arriving.

Roles are assigned at the start. Besides the presenter and reviewers there is a facilitator, who keeps time and enforces the protocol, and a note taker, who records feedback in a shared document. The presenter does not take notes, so they can listen properly.

The session opens with the presenter restating the goal and questions in two minutes. They then walk through the work without defending it. Reviewers may ask clarifying questions but not give feedback yet. The facilitator stops any feedback that slips in during this stage.

Next comes the silent round, in which reviewers write feedback individually. This is followed by sharing, where each reviewer reads out their notes in turn, without discussion, until all notes have been heard. Only then does open discussion begin, focused on the points that came up most often or that seem most important against the goal.

Feedback is expected to be specific and tied to the goal. Instead of saying a screen feels cluttered, a reviewer might say that the payment button competes with three other buttons of equal weight, so a first-time user may not see it. Reviewers are asked to describe the problem rather than prescribe a solution, unless the presenter has asked for suggestions.

The presenter closes the session by summarising what they heard and what they intend to try. They are free to reject feedback, but should say why. The note taker shares the notes within the hour.

Critiques of work at different stages need different emphasis. Early concept work is judged on whether it addresses the right problem and whether the core idea is sound. Later work is judged on detail, consistency and accessibility. The presenter states the stage at the start, and the facilitator steers reviewers away from pixel-level comments on early sketches, which waste time and discourage exploration. Reviewers who notice a serious accessibility barrier at any stage should always raise it, regardless of the stage, because such problems become harder to remove the longer they survive.

The studio uses a simple three-colour sticky note system during the silent round: one colour for things that work, one for things to rethink and one for open questions. Each reviewer gets exactly four notes of each colour, no more, which forces them to prioritise rather than list every small issue they notice. Unused notes are fine, and reviewers are told that leaving a colour empty is a valid signal in itself.

When critiques involve clients, facilitators spend a few minutes explaining the protocol and why it exists, because clients are often used to approving or rejecting work rather than shaping it. Senior client staff are asked to speak last in the sharing round so that others are not influenced by their views.

The protocol is reviewed every six months at a studio retrospective, and changes are trialled for a month before being adopted.

title: Accessibility audit of client services
note: An accessibility audit checks a website, app or physical service against accessibility guidelines and against the experience of disabled users. Wrenfold's audits combine automated checks, manual review with keyboard and screen reader, and short sessions with disabled participants. The output is a prioritised list of barriers and fixes.

title: Colour contrast at least 4.5 to 1
note: All body text in designs produced by the studio must have a contrast ratio of at least 4.5 to 1 against its background, and large headings at least 3 to 1. Brand colours that fail are adjusted or used only for decoration.

title: Custom form controls accessibility
note: Custom form controls, such as styled dropdowns, toggles and date pickers, often break keyboard navigation and screen reader announcements. The studio's pattern library documents accessible versions of each control, including focus behaviour, labels and error messages, so that clients' developers do not reinvent them badly.

title: Screen reader users excluded from testing
note: Usability tests often recruit only people who use a mouse or touch screen. Problems that block screen reader users therefore go unnoticed until after launch, when they are much more expensive to fix.

title: Recruit disabled participants for every study
note: Every research study run by the studio includes at least one disabled participant, and studies for public services include at least two. Recruitment budgets include the extra time and support this needs.

title: Participant sampling for research
note: Participant sampling is how the studio decides which and how many people to recruit for a study. Samples are built to cover the range of situations that matter for the service, such as age, digital confidence, language and access needs, rather than to be statistically representative of the whole population.

title: Recruit at least five participants per segment
note: For qualitative usability studies, each distinct user segment must have at least five participants. Fewer than that makes it hard to tell whether a problem is a pattern or one person's quirk.

title: Research recruitment and consent
note:
This note covers how Wrenfold recruits research participants and obtains their informed consent. Good recruitment is the foundation of useful research: the wrong participants produce confident findings about the wrong people. Consent is both a legal requirement and a matter of respect, because people are giving their time and often sharing personal experiences.

Recruitment starts from a screener, a short questionnaire that checks whether a potential participant fits the sample. Screener questions are written to avoid giving away the right answers, so people cannot easily talk their way in. The studio uses a mix of channels: client contact lists where people have agreed to be contacted, community organisations, social media posts and a specialist recruitment agency for harder-to-reach groups.

For public services, the studio makes a particular effort to recruit people who are often missed, such as those with low literacy, limited internet access, caring responsibilities or unusual working hours. This takes longer and costs more, and project plans allow for it from the start rather than treating it as a nice extra.

Every participant receives a plain-language information sheet before agreeing to take part. It explains who is running the research, who it is for, what will happen in the session, how long it will take, what will be recorded, how the information will be used and stored, and how to withdraw. The sheet is available in large print, easy read and the main community languages for the project.

Consent is recorded at the start of every session, even if a form was signed in advance. The researcher reads the key points aloud and asks the participant to confirm they are happy to continue. Participants are told they can skip any question, pause or stop at any time without giving a reason and still receive their thank-you payment.

Recordings and notes are stored in the studio's secure research folder, not on personal devices. Quotes used in reports are anonymised, and any detail that could identify a person in a small community is removed or changed. Raw recordings are deleted at the end of the engagement unless the participant agreed to longer use.

Session logistics are planned around participants rather than researchers. Sessions are offered at different times of day, in community venues as well as online, and travel costs are covered in advance where needed. Support workers, interpreters and companions are welcome, and their presence is noted in the session record.

No-shows are common in research and are planned for. Recruitment includes one or two reserve participants per round, who are paid for their time even if they are not needed. Reminder messages are sent the day before and on the morning of each session, using whatever channel the participant prefers, and the studio phone number is included so people can rearrange easily rather than simply not turning up.

Payment policy has two firm rules. Participants are thanked with grocery vouchers rather than cash or bank transfers, because vouchers can be handed over on the day without collecting bank details, and some participants on certain benefits have told us that cash payments cause them problems with reporting. And people under eighteen are never recruited unless a parent or guardian is present in the room for the whole session, not merely available nearby or on the phone.

Any concern about a participant's wellbeing during a session, such as distress or a disclosure of harm, is handled using the studio's safeguarding procedure, which takes priority over completing the research.

title: Five day design sprint format
note: The design sprint is an intensive workshop format that takes a team from a problem to a tested prototype in five days. Day one maps the problem, day two sketches solutions, day three decides, day four builds a prototype and day five tests it with users. Wrenfold uses it when a client needs a fast answer to one clear question.

title: Compress design sprints to four days for small clients
note: For small clients who cannot release staff for a full week, we run a four day version that merges mapping and sketching into one day. The trade-off is less time for the team to absorb the problem before sketching.

title: Workshop feedback loop
note: After every workshop, the studio collects feedback from participants and the client sponsor, reviews it in the next team meeting and updates its methods. This feedback loop is how facilitation practice improves over time rather than repeating the same mistakes.

title: Post-workshop participant survey
note: The post-workshop survey is a five-question form sent within a day of each workshop. It asks how useful the day was, which activity worked best, which worked least, whether people felt heard and what they would change.

title: Remote workshops over video
note: Remote workshops run entirely over video with a shared digital board. They allow participants from many locations to join, but require tighter agendas, more breaks and more explicit facilitation than sessions in a room.

title: Use a shared digital whiteboard for remote sessions
note: All remote workshops use a single shared digital whiteboard prepared in advance with frames for each activity. Participants are sent a short practice board a few days before so they can learn the basic tools.

title: Remote participants disengage
note: On video calls, people turn off cameras, check email and drift away from the activity. Facilitators may not notice until a group report-back reveals that half the table did nothing.

title: Breaks every 50 minutes in remote sessions
note: Remote sessions must include a break of at least ten minutes after every fifty minutes of activity. Screen fatigue builds faster than in a room, and longer stretches lead to poorer contributions.

title: Remote facilitation playbook
note:
The remote facilitation playbook gathers what Wrenfold has learned from running hundreds of workshops over video since the studio first had to move its practice online. Remote sessions can work as well as in-person ones, but only if the team accepts that they are a different format with their own rules rather than an in-person workshop squeezed onto a screen.

Agendas for remote sessions are shorter. A full in-person day becomes two half days, ideally on consecutive days so that momentum is not lost. Each activity is shorter and more tightly scoped, and the agenda includes buffers because technical problems always eat some time.

Preparation is heavier than for in-person work. The shared board is built in advance with a frame for every activity, clear instructions inside each frame and any templates already in place. Participants receive a practice board and a two-minute video explaining the tools they will need. The facilitators run a full dry run with colleagues playing participants a few days before.

Every remote session has at least three roles: a lead facilitator who guides the content, a supporting facilitator who watches the chat and the board and helps people who are stuck, and a producer who handles the technology. The producer starts the call early, manages breakout rooms, shares links, admits latecomers and fixes problems so that the facilitators can stay focused on the participants.

Openings are designed to get everyone speaking and using the tools within the first ten minutes. A quick check-in question that everyone answers aloud, followed by a simple board task such as placing a sticky note on a map, helps people get past the awkwardness of video.

Breakout rooms are used for small group work, with no more than five people in each. Every room has a clear task, a time limit and a named person who will report back. Facilitators visit rooms briefly to answer questions but avoid lingering, since their presence can change the conversation.

Engagement is monitored actively. The supporting facilitator watches who has not contributed on the board or in discussion and invites them in by name, gently, often by asking for their view on something they wrote. Cameras are encouraged but not required, because some participants have good reasons for keeping them off.

Accessibility needs are collected before every remote session. Some participants need captions, which are switched on by default. Others use screen readers that struggle with digital whiteboards, so the producer prepares an alternative way to contribute, such as typing into the chat or speaking to the supporting facilitator who adds notes for them. Slides and the board link are sent a day early so that anyone who needs more time to read can prepare. Participants on poor connections are offered a phone dial-in and a plain document version of each activity.

Behind the scenes, the facilitation team keeps a private backstage chat channel open throughout the session, separate from the participant chat, to coordinate timing, flag problems and agree changes to the plan without interrupting the room. The producer role is always held by someone who is not presenting anything that day, because the studio learned the hard way that a person sharing their screen cannot also rescue a frozen breakout room.

Closings in remote sessions are kept crisp: a quick summary on the board, the next steps and a short round of one-word reflections. The board is locked and exported immediately after the session so nothing is accidentally edited later.

title: How might we questions
note: How might we questions turn problems into open prompts for ideas. A pain point such as people miss their appointment letters becomes a question about how we might make sure people know when their appointment is. The wording invites many answers rather than one fix.

title: Affinity mapping of research notes
note: Affinity mapping groups many individual observations or ideas into clusters by similarity. Participants move sticky notes around a wall until patterns emerge, then name each cluster. It is the studio's standard way of making sense of large amounts of research data with a group.

title: Cluster sticky notes silently first
note: During affinity mapping, the first round of moving notes is done in silence. Talking too early leads to arguments about individual notes, while silent sorting lets patterns emerge before anyone defends a position.

title: Stakeholder interviews inside client organisations
note: Stakeholder interviews are one-to-one conversations with people inside the client organisation who influence or are affected by the project. They uncover goals, constraints, history and politics that would otherwise surprise the team later.

title: Should clients sit in on user interviews?
note: Clients often ask to watch user interviews. Seeing users first hand builds empathy and trust in the findings, but a client in the room can make participants guarded, especially when discussing a service the client runs. Should we allow observers, and under what rules?

title: Service blueprint method
note: A service blueprint extends a journey map by showing the front-stage actions staff take, the back-stage processes and the supporting systems behind each step. It helps clients see how internal changes would affect what users experience.

title: Magnetic blueprint wall in the studio
note: The blueprint wall is a large magnetic board in the studio used to build service blueprints with clients. Lanes are marked with tape and cards can be moved freely. Photographs are taken at the end of each session to record progress.

title: Usability testing with real people
note: Usability testing watches real people try to complete realistic tasks with a design while thinking aloud. It reveals where people get confused, make mistakes or give up. The studio usually tests with five to eight people per round and runs several rounds as the design evolves.

title: Usability test script guide
note:
The usability test script guide explains how Wrenfold writes and uses the scripts that moderators follow during usability sessions. A script keeps sessions consistent across participants and moderators, so that differences in results come from the design rather than from how the session was run. It also protects participants by making sure every session includes the same introductions, consent and debrief.

Every script has the same structure: welcome and consent, warm-up questions, tasks, follow-up questions and wrap-up. The welcome explains that the design is being tested, not the participant, and that there are no wrong answers. The moderator says that they did not create the design, even if they did, so that participants feel free to criticise.

Warm-up questions are about the participant's context, such as how they currently handle the task the service supports. These questions relax the participant and give the moderator background that helps interpret their behaviour later.

Tasks are written as realistic scenarios rather than instructions. Instead of telling someone to click the booking button, a task might describe a situation where they need to arrange a collection for an old fridge next week. Tasks avoid using the same words as the interface labels, because that turns the test into a word-matching game.

Each task has a clear end point, so the moderator knows when the participant has finished, and a note of what success looks like. The moderator records whether the task was completed, how long it took, where the participant hesitated and anything they said that stood out.

During tasks the moderator mostly stays quiet. If the participant goes silent, the moderator prompts them with neutral phrases asking what they are thinking. If they ask for help, the moderator turns the question back to them gently. Help is only given when the participant is completely stuck, and that is recorded as a failure for the task.

Follow-up questions explore what happened. The moderator asks about moments where the participant hesitated or seemed surprised, using their own words where possible. Questions are open and neutral, asking how something felt rather than whether it was good.

Scripts also cover what moderators do when things go wrong. If the prototype breaks, the moderator apologises, explains that it is the design's fault and moves on to the next task, noting where the break happened. If a participant becomes upset, the moderator pauses the session and checks whether they want to continue. If a participant reveals personal information unrelated to the task, the note taker leaves it out of the notes. Moderators carry a short card with these fallbacks so they do not have to remember them under pressure, and a second researcher is always available on call during remote sessions to step in if the moderator loses connection.

Two rules in the script are absolute. Moderators must never use the word easy in any question or prompt, either positively or negatively, because it pressures participants to say a task was simple even when they struggled. And the order of tasks is shuffled for every second participant, so that learning from earlier tasks does not always flatter the same later ones. The note taker keeps a record of which order each participant received.

Wrap-up thanks the participant, explains how their feedback will be used, answers any questions and confirms how their thank-you payment will be delivered. The script ends with a reminder to the moderator to stop recording only after the participant has left the call or room.

Scripts are piloted with a colleague before the first real session, and tasks that confuse the pilot participant are rewritten.

title: Think aloud protocol briefed with a practice task
note: Before the first real task in a usability session, participants practise thinking aloud on an unrelated simple activity, such as finding a recipe on a website. This warms them up and lets the moderator correct the habit of going silent.

title: Leading questions in moderation
note: Moderators under time pressure slip into leading questions, such as asking whether a button was clear. Participants tend to agree with the question's framing, so findings appear more positive than they should.

title: Synthesis of research findings
note: Synthesis is the work of turning raw research notes into findings and insights. The studio's synthesis sessions combine individual review of notes, affinity mapping and discussion until the team agrees on the most important patterns.

title: Synthesis within 48 hours of research
note: Synthesis sessions must happen within two days of the last research session in a round. Memory of the sessions fades quickly, and observations that were obvious in the room become unclear in notes a week later.

title: Writing insight statements
note: An insight statement captures a finding together with its explanation and implication for design, in one or two sentences. Good insights are specific, supported by evidence and suggest a direction without prescribing a solution.

title: Design principles for a client
note: For larger engagements the studio helps clients write a short set of design principles drawn from research. Principles guide decisions after the studio leaves, for example by reminding the client to write letters at a reading age most people can follow.

title: Workshop kit box
note: Every facilitator takes a standard kit box to in-person workshops. It contains sticky notes in four colours, thick markers, dot stickers, tape, timers, name labels, printed templates and spare batteries for the clicker.

title: Kit restocked after every workshop
note: The facilitator who used a kit box restocks it from the studio cupboard on their next working day and signs the checklist inside the lid. A half-empty box discovered on the morning of a workshop has happened too many times.

title: Workshop materials and room setup
note:
This note explains how Wrenfold chooses and prepares rooms and materials for in-person workshops. Facilitators often underestimate how much the physical environment shapes a session. A cramped, overheated room with nowhere to put sheets on the walls will drain energy no matter how good the agenda is.

Room selection starts with the agenda. The facilitator lists what each activity needs: table space for small groups, wall space for maps, an area where everyone can stand together and a place for refreshments away from the work. These needs are sent to the client when they offer a room, and the facilitator asks for photographs and a floor plan before agreeing.

Natural light and fresh air matter more than projectors. Rooms without windows are avoided where possible. If the only available room is poor, the facilitator adapts the agenda, for example by moving more activities to table work and shortening sessions.

Tables are arranged in small islands rather than a boardroom layout. Chairs should be light enough to move easily so that groups can reform. A spare table near the front holds the kit box and handouts.

Walls are prepared before participants arrive. Long sheets of paper are hung for maps and blueprints, with titles written in large letters. Facilitators check that the adhesive putty or tape will not damage the client's paintwork, after an embarrassing incident with freshly decorated walls at a client's office.

Materials are prepared from the kit box and any session-specific printouts. Templates are printed at large sizes so that groups can work on them together. Markers are tested and dried-out ones thrown away. Sticky notes are chosen in colours that remain readable for people with common forms of colour blindness.

Accessibility is checked for every room. The facilitator confirms step-free access, accessible toilets, a hearing loop if needed, and quiet space for anyone who needs a break from the group. Participants are asked in advance about access needs, and adjustments are made without anyone having to explain themselves in front of others.

Refreshments are arranged with the client. Food arrives at a set time away from the main work area so that breaks are real breaks. Dietary needs are collected with the access questions.

Facilitators arrive at least ninety minutes before the start. This time is used to arrange tables, hang sheets, test any screens, check the temperature and walk the route from reception so that directions can be given clearly. A sign at reception and at any confusing corridor junction helps participants find the room without stress.

There are two firm room rules. The studio avoids rooms with glass walls on more than one side, because people outside watching the session make participants self-conscious and because sticky notes do not hold on glass for long. And any room booked for a full-day workshop must offer at least 6 metres of clear, continuous wall space for the main map, since splitting a journey across separate short walls breaks the flow of the work.

At the end of the day the room is cleared, all materials are photographed and rolled for transport, and the room is left as it was found. Any damage or problems with the room are reported to the client the same day, and notes on the room are added to the studio's venue list so that future facilitators know what to expect.

title: Ideation methods for groups
note: Ideation methods help groups generate many ideas quickly before judging them. The studio uses a small set of well-understood methods so participants spend their energy on ideas rather than on learning new rules each time.

title: Crazy eights exercise
note: In the crazy eights exercise, each participant folds a sheet into eight panels and sketches eight different ideas in eight minutes. The time pressure stops people from perfecting one idea and pushes them past their first obvious thought.

title: Dot voting on options
note: Dot voting lets a group show preferences by placing a limited number of sticky dots on the options they favour. It gives a quick visual picture of where the group's interest lies, though it is not a decision on its own.

title: Dot voting favours popular early ideas
note: When people vote at the same time on a wall, they see where others have placed dots and follow the crowd. Ideas posted early or near the centre tend to gather more votes regardless of merit.

title: Use weighted voting with a decider
note: After dot voting, a named decider, usually the client sponsor, makes the final choice and explains their reasoning to the group. Votes inform the decision but do not make it, which avoids watered-down compromises.

title: Inclusive design as core practice
note: Inclusive design means designing for the full range of people who will use a service, including disabled people, older people, people with low literacy and people using assistive technology. The studio treats it as a core part of every project, not a separate checklist at the end.

title: Workshop materials available in large print
note: Handouts, templates and agendas for every in-person workshop must be available in large print on request, and at least two large print copies are brought to every session whether or not anyone has asked.

title: Should we offer sign language interpretation by default?
note: At present interpreters are booked only when a participant requests one. Offering interpretation by default for public workshops would signal welcome to Deaf participants but adds significant cost. Should the default change?

title: Design system handover
note: When an engagement produces interface designs, the studio hands them over to the client's developers as a small design system: colours, type, spacing, components and usage guidance, along with the reasoning behind key choices.

title: Component library documentation
note: The component library documentation describes each interface component in the handover, with examples, states, accessibility notes and when not to use it. It is written for developers and for future designers joining the client team.

title: Client readout at engagement end
note: The client readout is the closing presentation of an engagement, where the studio shares findings, recommendations and next steps with sponsors and the wider client team. It is often the only part of the work that senior leaders see directly.

title: Readout presentation structure
note:
This note describes how Wrenfold structures the final readout presentation at the end of a client engagement. The readout has to do several jobs at once: summarise weeks of work for people who were not involved, make the evidence feel real, recommend clear actions and leave the client motivated rather than defensive. A consistent structure makes this easier to achieve and easier to prepare under deadline pressure.

The presentation opens with the question the engagement set out to answer, stated in one sentence, and a reminder of who was involved: how many people took part in research, which teams joined workshops and what was produced along the way. This establishes that the findings rest on real evidence.

Next comes a short story of one person's experience, usually a composite drawn from research and clearly labelled as such. The story walks through the journey and its main pain points in under three minutes. Leaders often remember the story long after they forget the slides that follow.

Findings follow, typically between four and seven of them. Each finding has its own slide with a plain statement, a short explanation, a direct quote from a participant and, where relevant, a number or small chart. The team resists the urge to include every finding, putting minor ones in an appendix.

The studio then shows the journey map or blueprint at a high level, with the pain points behind each finding highlighted, so that the audience can see how the findings connect across the service.

Recommendations are grouped into quick wins, medium changes and larger strategic shifts. Each recommendation names a likely owner on the client side and a first step that could happen within a month. Vague advice such as improve communication is not allowed.

Visual style is restrained. Slides use large type, few words and real photographs from research where participants agreed. Charts are simple and labelled directly rather than with legends.

Questions from senior leaders are anticipated during preparation. The team lists the ten questions they most expect, including hostile ones, and agrees who will answer each and what evidence they will point to. Where the honest answer is that the research did not cover something, the team says so plainly and suggests how it could be found out. Clients have told us that this frankness builds more trust than a confident answer that later turns out to be wrong.

Length is managed carefully. The core presentation runs for about thirty minutes, leaving time for discussion. If the material does not fit, the team cuts findings rather than speaking faster. A one-page summary handout is prepared for anyone who arrives late or needs to brief colleagues afterwards.

There is one fixed element of the structure that clients sometimes find surprising. Every readout includes a single slide titled with an uncomfortable truth: the finding the client is least likely to want to hear, such as a policy causing harm or a team working against users. That slide is always shown before the recommendations, never after them, so that the recommendations are heard as a response to it rather than the uncomfortable truth being lost at the end when attention has faded.

The presentation closes with next steps, a thank you to everyone involved and time for questions. The full deck, research appendix and raw artefacts are shared the same day.

Rehearsal is mandatory. The team runs the full readout at least once internally, timed, with a colleague playing a sceptical senior client.

title: Readouts limited to 45 minutes
note: Final readouts are capped at forty-five minutes including questions. Senior audiences lose focus in longer sessions, and a tight limit forces the team to choose what really matters. Detailed walkthroughs are offered separately to working teams.

title: Workshop pricing by day
note: The studio prices workshops by day, including preparation and write-up time, rather than by the hour in the room. Preparation and synthesis typically take two to three times as long as the workshop itself.

title: Should we run open public workshops?
note: Some designers want to run paid public workshops teaching studio methods to people from many organisations. This could bring income and new clients, but takes time away from client work and needs different marketing.

title: Facilitator training path
note: New studio staff learn facilitation through reading, observing experienced facilitators, co-facilitating and finally leading with support. Feedback after each session is specific and written down so progress can be tracked.

title: New facilitators co-facilitate three workshops first
note: Before leading a client workshop alone, a new facilitator must co-facilitate at least three, each with a different senior colleague. They then lead one with a senior colleague in the supporting role.

title: Energisers and warm-ups
note: Energisers are short activities used at the start of a workshop or after a break to lift energy and get people talking. The studio prefers warm-ups linked to the topic, such as sharing a recent experience of the service, over games with no connection to the work.

title: Warm-ups feel patronising to senior clients
note: Senior client staff sometimes see playful warm-ups as a waste of their time and disengage for the rest of the day. A poorly judged energiser can damage the facilitator's credibility in the first ten minutes.

title: Co-design with frontline staff
note: Co-design involves the people who deliver a service day to day in shaping its redesign. Frontline staff know where processes break and what users ask about, and changes they helped create are far more likely to stick.

title: Pay frontline participants for their time
note: Where frontline staff join workshops outside their normal duties, the studio asks the client to pay overtime or give time off in lieu. Expecting people to contribute unpaid signals that their knowledge is valued less than that of managers.

title: Customer call notes overview
note: Customer call notes record conversations between Corvane's customer success team and Tallyport customers. Notes capture who was on the call, what they raised, what we promised and any follow-up. They are the shared memory of each account, so that anyone picking it up can see the history without asking around.

title: Marrow Freight account
note: Marrow Freight is a regional haulage and depot maintenance company with around 300 Tallyport users, one of our largest accounts. They use scheduling for depot mechanics and invoicing for third-party repair work. Month end is their critical period because invoices for the whole month are raised in two days.

title: Call with Marrow Freight about month end outage
note: Marrow Freight's finance manager called after invoices failed to generate for several hours on the last working day of the month. Their team stayed late to finish by hand. She wants a written explanation, credit for the lost time and a promise that we will avoid deploys during their month end window. We agreed to send the incident summary within two days.

title: Marrow Freight wants bulk invoice export
note: Marrow Freight asked for a way to export all invoices for a month in one file for their accounting system. Today their clerk downloads them one at a time, which takes most of a morning. They would accept a zipped folder of PDFs plus a summary spreadsheet.

title: Quarterly business review with Marrow Freight
note:
These notes cover the quarterly business review with Marrow Freight held at their head office. Attending from their side were the operations director, the finance manager, the depot systems lead and two depot supervisors. From Corvane, the account manager, the customer success manager and a product manager joined, with a solutions engineer dialling in for the integration discussion.

The review opened with usage figures. Active users have grown by about fifteen percent over the quarter, mostly from the two depots that joined after the pilot. Job completion through the mobile app is now above ninety percent, up from seventy at the start of the year, which the operations director credited to the supervisors pushing paper job cards out of the depots. Invoice volume is steady, but the time from job completion to invoice has dropped from six days to two.

The finance manager raised the month end outage again. She acknowledged the incident summary we sent but said her team still felt exposed, because month end is when they most need the system and when they have the least room to recover. She asked for a formal commitment that we will not deploy during their last two working days. The account manager explained that we cannot freeze the whole platform for one customer but offered to share the release calendar and flag any release that touches invoicing in advance.

The depot systems lead walked through their integration with the parts inventory system. It works, but failures are silent: if a parts record fails to sync, nobody is told and the invoice goes out without the parts cost. The solutions engineer agreed to look at whether our webhook retries and failure notifications can help, and to review their integration logs together next month.

The supervisors talked about the mobile app. They like the new schedule board but complained that technicians in two depots with weak signal lose photos when the app is closed before upload finishes. The product manager explained that the offline work in progress should help and offered to enrol those depots in the beta.

Feature requests were reviewed. Bulk invoice export remains their top ask. Second is the ability to group jobs by vehicle rather than by customer site, because much of their work is on their own fleet. Third is better reporting on technician utilisation for their quarterly board pack.

Commercially, the renewal is in five months. The operations director said renewal is likely but that the board will ask about reliability, and that a competitor has approached them. The account manager will prepare a reliability summary for their board and propose a two-year term with a price hold.

The meeting ended with a short tour of the main depot, where the supervisors showed how job cards are now displayed on a wall screen in the workshop. Mechanics check it at the start of each shift instead of collecting paper from the office, which the supervisors said has reduced arguments about who was meant to do what.

A note on contacts and preferences for whoever handles this account. The operations director, Bettina Crale, wants outage alerts sent by text message to her mobile rather than by email, because she does not read email outside office hours. She also asks that nobody phones her before ten in the morning, since she spends the early hours walking the depots. The finance manager prefers email and a written summary after every call.

Actions: send the release calendar monthly; investigate silent parts sync failures; enrol two depots in the offline beta; prepare the reliability summary; schedule the next review for the same month next quarter.

title: Marrow Freight escalation to executive sponsor
note: After the month end outage, Marrow Freight's operations director bypassed support and wrote directly to our chief operating officer, who is their executive sponsor. This customer escalation means the account now has executive attention, and every update must be copied to the sponsor until the director confirms she is satisfied.

title: Marrow Freight renewal at risk
note: With a competitor approaching them and the outage still fresh, Marrow Freight's renewal is less certain than its usage suggests. Losing them would cost a meaningful share of annual revenue and a valuable reference in the haulage sector.

title: Hollins Dairy account
note: Hollins Dairy is a farm cooperative that runs a fleet of milk collection tankers and an on-farm equipment servicing team. They have about forty Tallyport users. Their engineers service milking equipment on member farms, often in remote areas with poor signal.

title: Hollins Dairy migration from spreadsheets
note: Hollins Dairy is moving its service history, equipment register and customer list from a set of shared spreadsheets into Tallyport. The spreadsheets contain years of inconsistent data. The migration is being done in stages, one region of farms at a time, with our onboarding specialist cleaning the data before each import.

title: Hollins Dairy asks for route optimisation
note: The Hollins Dairy service coordinator asked whether Tallyport can suggest the most efficient order of farm visits for each engineer. Engineers currently plan their own routes and often cross the same valleys twice in a day. We explained route suggestions are on the roadmap but not yet scheduled.

title: Can Hollins Dairy get a discount for annual prepay?
note: Hollins Dairy's treasurer asked whether paying for the year upfront would earn a discount, since the cooperative has cash after the spring milk price review. Our standard terms do not include a prepay discount, so this needs a decision from sales leadership.

title: Hollins Dairy contact preferences
note: The Hollins Dairy service coordinator prefers phone calls to email and is easiest to reach between milking times, roughly late morning and early afternoon. Their treasurer only joins calls about billing and asks for an agenda in advance.

title: Darnley Clinics account
note: Darnley Clinics is a group of private physiotherapy and podiatry clinics that uses Tallyport to schedule home visits by clinicians and to invoice patients and insurers. They are sensitive about privacy because notes may mention health conditions.

title: Darnley Clinics onboarding call series
note:
These notes summarise the series of onboarding calls with Darnley Clinics over their first six weeks as a Tallyport customer. Darnley runs eleven clinics and a home visit service, and they chose Tallyport mainly to manage home visits, which were previously booked through a shared calendar and paper forms. The onboarding team included our onboarding specialist, a customer success manager and, for two calls, a solutions engineer.

The first call set goals. Darnley wanted all home visits scheduled in Tallyport within a month, invoices to patients and insurers generated automatically, and clinicians able to complete visit forms on tablets. Their practice manager led from their side and was clear that clinicians are busy and will reject anything that adds clicks to their day.

The second call covered configuration. We set up visit types, durations, clinician skills and travel zones. Darnley's insurers each require different invoice details, so we created invoice templates per insurer. The practice manager was surprised at how many settings exist and asked for a simple written record of every choice made, which we provided.

The third call was about forms. Clinicians record a short set of structured observations and a free text note at each visit. We built the form in Tallyport's form builder and tested it with two clinicians, who asked for larger tick boxes and fewer mandatory fields. Both changes were made the same day.

The fourth call dealt with data and privacy. Darnley's data protection officer joined and asked where data is stored, who at Corvane can access it, how long it is kept and what happens if they leave. We walked through our security documentation and data processing terms. She asked for a written answer on several points, which we sent the following week.

The fifth call was a go-live review. Three clinics were live and the rest followed within a fortnight. Clinicians reported that the tablet app was quick, but some found the sync indicator confusing and thought visits had not saved. We agreed to add a short tip to their training material.

The sixth call closed onboarding. Darnley rated the experience highly but raised two follow-up items: the invoice PDF layout for one insurer, and a request to organise uploaded documents such as referral letters into folders per patient.

Support patterns during onboarding were typical. Most tickets were about permissions, such as receptionists seeing more than they should, and about the sync indicator. One clinic had tablets with an old operating system that could not run the app, and Darnley replaced them. The practice manager praised the speed of replies but asked that support avoid technical jargon with clinic staff, who are not used to software terms and find them off-putting.

Practical notes for the account team. Darnley requires that anything resembling clinical notes stays in our regional data centre for their country, which their contract states explicitly, so any support request involving data export must check the region first. Their IT lead, Ruben Askew, insists on a written summary of every call within one working day, and he will chase if it does not arrive. He prefers bullet points to long paragraphs and wants actions listed with an owner and a date.

The account now moves to the standard success cadence, with a monthly check-in for the first quarter and quarterly reviews after that.

title: Darnley Clinics document filing by folder
note: Darnley Clinics asked for referral letters, consent forms and scan images to be filed into folders per patient inside Tallyport. Today all uploads sit in a flat list on each customer record, and clinicians struggle to find the right letter. Folder-based filing would mirror how their clinics organise paper records.

title: Darnley Clinics complaint about invoice PDF layout
