title: Quenby Plumbing renewal negotiation
note:
These notes cover three calls with Quenby Plumbing about their renewal, which falls due at the end of the next quarter. Quenby has been a customer for four years and is generally positive about the product, but they were approached by a competitor offering a lower price and a stronger stock management module. Their managing director led the negotiation, joined by the operations manager and, on the final call, their accountant.

The first call was exploratory. The managing director explained that the competitor had offered a price about twenty percent lower for the first two years and had demonstrated stock features that impressed the operations manager. He was candid that he did not want the disruption of switching, but that he needed either a better price or a clearer product direction to justify staying.

We listened more than we pitched. The operations manager described their stock problems in detail: engineers do not always record parts used, vans run out of common fittings, and the office cannot see what stock sits in which van. Some of this is a process issue rather than a software issue, which he acknowledged.

The second call brought in our product manager for stock and mobile. She showed the roadmap for van stock, which includes barcode scanning, automatic reorder suggestions and better reporting. She was careful not to promise dates for items that were not yet scheduled. The operations manager was most interested in barcode scanning, because their engineers already carry phones and their main supplier labels all parts with barcodes.

The managing director also raised the offline issues his engineers face and the March outage. We explained the offline improvements in progress and offered to include Quenby in the beta. He accepted, saying that seeing progress would matter more to him than slides.

Before the third call, our account manager prepared options: a one-year renewal at the current price, or a two-year renewal with a price hold and a modest discount in year two. Sales leadership approved both. We decided not to try to match the competitor's price directly, because the real issue for Quenby was the stock features.

The third call included their accountant, who checked the terms and asked about payment schedules. Quenby prefers quarterly invoicing, which we agreed. The managing director then put forward his own proposal, which became the basis of the deal.

The accountant also raised the question of what happens to their data and history if they ever do leave. We explained the export process and confirmed that there is no charge for it. This seemed to reassure him more than any discount, and he said it made the decision to stay feel less like a trap.

The agreed outcome is a two-year renewal at the current price with the year-two discount, on one condition. If the technician app does not support barcode scanning of parts by the end of the third quarter, Quenby may leave at the end of year one without penalty. This condition is recorded in a side letter signed by our head of sales, not in the main contract, so the account manager must keep the side letter with the account records and remind the product team of the date.

Actions: send the renewal paperwork and side letter; enrol Quenby in the offline beta; schedule a stock workshop with the operations manager next month.

title: Tolland Facilities expansion call
note:
These notes cover a call with Tolland Facilities about expanding their use of Tallyport. Tolland has grown through acquisitions, buying smaller maintenance firms in different regions and gradually moving them onto shared systems. The call included their head of operations, their head of IT, a regional director from one of the acquired firms and, from Corvane, the account manager, the customer success manager and a solutions engineer.

The head of operations opened by explaining their strategy. Each acquired firm currently runs its own scheduling system, some of them on paper. Tolland wants every region on Tallyport within eighteen months so that they can share engineers across regions, report consistently to clients and reduce the number of systems they pay for.

The regional director described his firm's current setup and his worries. His engineers are used to a simple tool and are wary of change. He wants to keep some local job types and price lists that differ from Tolland's standard. We explained how Tallyport supports regional settings within a single account, which reassured him.

The head of IT focused on integration and security. Tolland's finance system is central and receives invoice data from Tallyport every night. Each new region will need its own cost centres mapped. He also asked about single sign-on for the acquired firms, which have separate directories, and about audit logs showing who changed what.

The solutions engineer walked through how multiple directories can be connected and how audit logs can be exported. He also raised capacity, since Tolland's scheduling board would grow considerably, and confirmed that the team had tested boards of that size.

We discussed training. Tolland would like a train-the-trainer approach, where we train a few champions in each region who then train their colleagues. They also asked for short videos in plain language for engineers who will not attend formal training.

Pricing was discussed in outline only. The account manager explained volume tiers and agreed to send a proposal. The head of operations asked that the proposal separate the cost of new seats from any services such as data migration and training, so they can budget them from different lines.

Migration of existing data was the last topic before commercials. Some acquired firms hold years of job history and asset records that clients rely on for compliance. Tolland would like this history available in Tallyport rather than archived elsewhere. The onboarding specialist explained the import tools and the data cleaning usually needed, and suggested a trial import from one firm to estimate effort. The regional director offered his firm's data for that trial, since its records are reasonably tidy and its client list is small enough to check by hand.

The scale of the expansion was the key commercial point of the call. Tolland plans to add 140 technician seats in their northern region first, before any other acquired firm moves across. However, that rollout is conditional on a clear written answer about whether data for those engineers' clients can be kept within their region, because two of the northern firm's largest clients are public bodies with strict data location rules. The head of IT wants this answer before their next board meeting.

Actions: confirm regional data residency options in writing; send a priced proposal with seats and services separated; share training materials and video examples; schedule a technical session on directory integration.

title: Garnet Pest Services churn interview
note:
These notes record the exit interview with Garnet Pest Services after they gave notice that they would not renew their Tallyport subscription. The interview was held by video with Garnet's operations lead and their finance director. Our customer success manager led, with the account manager listening. The aim was to understand honestly why they were leaving and whether anything could have changed the outcome.

The operations lead started by saying the decision was not personal and that her team had liked working with us. She described the past year: they had grown to around fifty users, used the recurring visit features heavily, and found the mobile app reliable. Technicians in particular were sorry to lose it, because the replacement system they are moving to has a weaker mobile experience.

We asked about frustrations. The biggest was chemical usage reporting. Regulators and large clients increasingly ask pest control firms to show exactly what was used where, and Garnet had asked us for a report more than once. We had explained that their data was entered as free text and suggested changing their forms, but the change had been made late and the report still did not exist.

The second frustration was price. Their finance director said our per-seat pricing became expensive as they added seasonal technicians for the summer peak, and our minimum term made it hard to scale seats down in winter. She suggested that seasonal seat pricing would suit many trades businesses.

The third point was support response times. Most issues were solved well, but two urgent issues during the busy season waited more than a day for a reply. The operations lead accepted that both were complex but said that a quick acknowledgement with an honest estimate would have made a difference.

We asked whether any of these alone would have caused them to leave. Both said no. Each was an irritation, and together they made the business case for staying weaker, but none was decisive.

The operations lead also mentioned that her technicians had built informal habits around the app, such as photographing bait stations at every visit, which the replacement system will not support as easily. She wondered whether they would lose some of the discipline those habits had created, and said she would try to keep them going on paper if necessary.

They were then asked directly what tipped the decision. The finance director explained that they had been acquired by a larger group the previous autumn. The new parent company requires every subsidiary to use a single shared field service platform chosen at group level, regardless of how well the current tools work. The real reason for leaving was that mandate, not any product gap. She added, unprompted, that the parent's contract for that platform runs until 2028, and that if it is not renewed then, Garnet would push to come back to us.

We thanked them and confirmed the data export process. Actions: send the export within the agreed period; record seasonal seat pricing as a product suggestion; log chemical reporting as a lost-deal feature ask; set a reminder to contact Garnet before the parent's platform contract ends. The success manager will also share the interview notes with the support and pricing teams, and will send a short personal thank-you note to the operations lead, whose candour made this one of the most useful exit interviews of the year.

title: Account handover notes for Kestle Joinery
note:
These handover notes were written by the departing customer success manager for Kestle Joinery, so that the new manager can pick up the account smoothly. Kestle is a bespoke joinery business that makes and fits kitchens, staircases and built-in furniture. They have about thirty Tallyport users across their workshop and fitting teams and have been a customer for two years.

Kestle's use of Tallyport is a little unusual. Most of their jobs are long projects rather than short visits, so they use the scheduling board to plan fitting days over several weeks and the job forms to record measurements, materials and snags. Invoices are raised in stages: a deposit, a payment on delivery of materials and a final payment after fitting.

The owner founded the business and still makes most decisions, but he rarely joins calls now. Day-to-day contact is with the operations coordinator, who is organised, friendly and quick to reply. She likes a short monthly check-in and prefers that issues are raised by email first so she can look into them before a call.

Their main asks over the past year have been timesheet integration, so that hours recorded in Tallyport flow into their payroll system, and better support for multi-stage invoices. The second has been partly addressed by the new invoice designer beta, which they joined. They have given useful feedback and should stay in the beta.

There have been two difficult moments. Early in the relationship, a misconfigured invoice template sent final invoices before fitting was complete, upsetting several of their customers. We fixed it quickly and offered a credit, and the coordinator has since been generous about it. More recently, the March sync outage left fitters unable to record snags, which mattered because snags drive their final invoices.

Kestle is healthy overall. Usage is steady, support tickets are low and they renewed last year without negotiation. They are a good candidate for a case study about project-based work, though nobody has asked them yet.

Their workshop manager is an occasional but important contact. He joins calls only when something affects production planning, such as changes to how materials are recorded on job forms. He dislikes video calls and prefers to talk on the phone while walking the workshop floor. When he does raise an issue, it is usually well founded and worth acting on quickly.

On the commercial side, the account is on a standard plan with an annual term. There is no price hold, so this year's list price increase will apply at renewal, and the new manager should mention it at a regular check-in well before renewal rather than letting it arrive as a surprise on an invoice.

Some practical points the new manager needs. Kestle's finance contact is Imogen Pardew, who works part time and must be copied on any conversation that touches price, contract terms or invoices, even informally, because she has complained in the past about learning of changes second hand. In addition, during last year's renewal the previous account manager made a verbal promise that Kestle's new hires would receive free onboarding training for the life of the contract. It was never written down, but Kestle remembers it, so it should be honoured and ideally confirmed in writing.

Open actions: follow up on timesheet integration options; check beta feedback on multi-stage invoices; consider asking about a case study at the next check-in.

title: Price increase call debrief
note:
This debrief summarises what account managers heard during the round of calls to explain the annual price increase to Tallyport customers. Over four weeks the team spoke to nearly two hundred accounts, from single-van businesses to the largest enterprise customers. The aim of the debrief is to capture reactions, objections and outcomes so that next year's approach can improve.

Overall reactions were calmer than feared. Most customers accepted the increase, especially when the account manager could point to concrete improvements from the past year, such as the new schedule board and faster invoice generation. Customers who had been involved in betas were the most accepting, because they had seen the work behind the changes.

The most common objection was timing. Several customers said the increase landed during a difficult trading period for trades businesses, with material costs rising and margins thin. Account managers who acknowledged this directly and did not argue the point found the conversations went better.

The second objection was about value for features they did not use. Customers who use only scheduling felt they were paying for invoicing and reporting they did not need. This fed into an ongoing conversation about lighter plans for smaller customers.

Large accounts mostly asked about price holds in exchange for longer terms. Several were offered two-year renewals with the new price fixed for the term, and most accepted. A few asked for the increase to be delayed until their next renewal date, which was standard practice anyway.

Communication method mattered. Customers who heard about the increase first by phone, with an email confirmation afterwards, were noticeably happier than those who received an email first. Next year the team plans to call every account above a certain size before any written notice goes out.

A handful of customers were angry, usually because the increase arrived alongside an unresolved support issue. In these cases account managers were told to fix the issue first and only then return to the price conversation.

Churn attributable to the increase so far is low, but it is too early to judge, since many renewals are months away.

Account managers also noticed which customers asked the most detailed questions. Finance contacts wanted exact figures, effective dates and how the change would appear on invoices. Operations contacts were more interested in whether the increase would pay for features they had requested. Preparing a short sheet with both kinds of answer helped later calls go faster, and several managers suggested making it standard next year. The sheet should also include the percentage change for each plan, since some customers worked it out wrongly and became alarmed at a figure much larger than the real one.

The concession agreed for small customers deserves a precise record, because it has already caused confusion. Accounts with fewer than ten seats were grandfathered at their old price for twelve months, but only if the customer confirmed acceptance of the new terms before 30 November. Customers who confirmed after that date moved to the new price at their next billing cycle, and account managers have no discretion to extend the deadline without approval from the head of customer success.

Recommendations for next year include earlier notice, phone-first communication for larger accounts, and pairing the announcement with a clear summary of the year's improvements. The debrief will be shared with sales and product so that pricing and packaging discussions start from what customers actually said.

title: Support ticket trends from calls
note: Success managers note which support issues come up during their calls, even if the customer has not raised a ticket. These notes reveal problems customers have learned to work around and no longer bother reporting.

title: Customer training requests
note: Customers frequently ask for training when they hire new office staff or when features change. Requests range from a single new hire needing an overview to whole teams wanting a refresher on scheduling.

title: Offer monthly group training webinars
note: Instead of one-to-one training for every request, we run monthly group webinars on core topics, recorded for later viewing. One-to-one sessions remain available for enterprise customers and for unusual setups.

title: Data export requests on cancellation
note: When customers cancel, they usually ask for a full export of their data so they can move it to another system or keep it for their records. The export includes jobs, customers, invoices and attachments.

title: Export provided within 10 days of cancellation
note: A complete data export must be delivered to the customer within ten working days of a cancellation request, in standard file formats, and the customer must confirm they received it before their data is deleted.

note: Reference customers agree to speak to prospects about their experience with Tallyport. The success team keeps a list of willing references by industry and size and makes sure no single customer is asked too often.

title: Will Brisco Electrical act as a reference?
note: Brisco's office manager was very positive about the schedule board and agreed to a marketing quote. Would she also take calls from prospects in the electrical trade? We should ask at the next check-in rather than assume.

title: Feature ask for technician location sharing
note: Several customers asked whether the office could see engineers' live locations on a map, to answer customer questions about arrival times and to assign urgent jobs to the nearest person.

title: Privacy concerns from technicians about location sharing
note: Some engineers at customer firms dislike the idea of being tracked, particularly outside working hours. Location features without clear limits could provoke staff complaints or legal challenges for our customers.

title: Upsell conversations for the reporting add-on
note: Accounts that frequently export data into spreadsheets are good candidates for the reporting add-on. Success managers raise it when a customer mentions spending hours building their own reports.

title: Call with Hollins Dairy about missed delivery reminders
note: Hollins Dairy reported that farmers were not receiving the automatic text reminders before engineer visits. The cause was that many farm phone numbers were stored as landlines during the spreadsheet import. We helped them identify and update the mobile numbers.
